un-ga-res-46:
Rebuilding the lands smashed by war was the great task facing the world in 1946. Resolution 46 of the General Assembly, passed on 11 December 1946, takes note of a first report on the rebuilding of devastated areas. It backs the plans of the Economic and Social Council. Those plans call for a survey of rebuilding needs in Asia and the Far East, and for study work in Europe to keep going.

All who can help are urged to act. Member states, the council, aid bodies, and world agencies should take every step in their power toward swift fixes. The Assembly also directs a word to the new World Bank: swift loans for rebuilding would serve the common good.
un-ga-res-a-69-46: Trust built close to home is the theme of Resolution A/69/46, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The vote recalls a chain of Assembly texts since 2003 on trust-building steps at the level of regions and sub-regions. It also recalls the 2003 call for states to settle their rows by peaceful means, as the Charter's sixth chapter sets out. Such steps, the Assembly has long held, work best when states craft them for their own ground.

plos-pone-0000046:
Alon Goren, Giora Simchen, Eitan Fibach, and co-authors studied the fine control of the genes that make hemoglobin in a 2006 paper. Globin genes produce the protein chains that carry oxygen in red blood cells. Their output must be tuned with care: too little causes anemia, and the wrong type at the wrong age causes disease.

DNA methylation, chemical tags placed on DNA, provides part of that tuning. The team showed methylation fine-tunes globin gene expression rather than simply switching it off. Fine control, not just on and off, is how the body shifts globin types from fetus to adult. The finding adds detail to a classic model of gene regulation with direct links to blood disorders.

The President's Log continues with the Cairo days, 22 to 25 November 1943, kept hour by hour. It opens with Roosevelt's flight from Tunis on 22 November, which ran late and worried the welcoming party at Cairo West airport.

Two fighter groups missed their rendezvous with the President's plane, which had swung south to the Nile and flown up the river over the Sphinx and the Pyramids. Roosevelt settled at Ambassador Kirk's villa near Gizeh, while the Sextant Conference met at the Mena House Hotel by the Pyramids. Churchill and the Chiangs, who had arrived the day before, called that afternoon, and a first meeting with staffs ran from nine until after eleven that night.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d346:
Alexander Kirk sent Harry Hopkins a second urgent, secret telegram from Cairo on 29 November 1943 about the held Cairo communiqué. It follows his alarmed message of the day before on the release arrangements.

The Chinese chargé has just called on Kirk to say he has cabled the text to Chungking, with orders to hold release until his own flash. Kirk reminded him that he, Kirk, was charged with giving the notice once word came from Tehran. Process rewards improve Verilog generation. Vijayaraghavan improved RTL synthesis with LLMs. Semiconductor design needs LLM assistance. Vijayaraghavan's StepPRM automates chip design.
arxiv-2606-04546: Bivariate inverse Gaussian degradation processes were modeled with shared random effects for fatigue applications. The reliability statistics were derived. The finding serves engineering. Degradation models predict fatigue failure. Yuvraj Dutta modeled fatigue degradation. Aerospace needs fatigue life prediction. Dutta's processes schedule predictive maintenance.
arxiv-2606-04946: Choosing the best small set from many options — with each extra pick worth less than the last — is a problem that shows up in marketing, sensor placement, and data summarization. This paper gives a general framework for doing it when the options keep changing over time while staying consistent with earlier choices. It turns a messy moving-target problem into one with reliable guarantees.
arxiv-2606-05146: In March 2026 a gamma-ray burst designated GRB 260310A flashed unusually faint in gamma rays — yet its afterglow shone brightly across other wavelengths. This paper reports early multiwavelength observations of that afterglow, source AT 2026fgk, caught independently of the gamma-ray trigger. The mismatch between faint burst and luminous afterglow challenges simple models of how these cosmic explosions work.
arxiv-2606-05646: AI coding assistants forget: each session starts fresh, repeating old mistakes. This paper enhances software engineering through closed-loop memory optimization — agents that remember what worked, compress the lessons, and reuse them. Memory that improves itself turns a forgetful assistant into an accumulating expert.
arxiv-2606-06146: Stack two Janus monolayers — sheets with different faces — and magnetism emerges that neither sheet has alone. This paper finds stacking-dependent magnetism and tunable half-metallicity in bilayer Janus 1T-MnSSe: materials conducting only one electron spin. Twist-controlled magnetism is a dream for spintronic devices.
arxiv-2606-06346: Optimal transport — moving mass as cheaply as possible — spawns endless variants of conditional quantities and cost functionals. This paper unifies them with single formulas covering the whole family. Unification turns a sprawling toolkit into one coherent and complete instrument.
arxiv-2606-06546: Grading AI tutors in niche educational topics — the long tail — needs rubrics nobody has written. Elmes+ constructs fine-grained evaluation rubrics automatically for those scenarios. Automated rubrics bring rigorous evaluation to education's forgotten corners. Long-tail topics finally get the assessment they deserve.
arxiv-2606-06646: Good arguments have structure — claims, evidence, rebuttals — that most text lacks explicitly. CAF-Gen enriches argumentation structures with a multi-agent system: agents debating to flesh out the reasoning. The enriched structures make arguments machine-readable and human-improvable. Structured debate becomes computable.
arxiv-2606-06746: Deep reinforcement learning is notoriously flaky — same code, wildly different results across runs. This paper studies performance variation in deep RL: where the instability comes from and how to measure it. Understanding the variance is the first step to taming it.
arxiv-2606-07046: Cloud systems that scale predictively — before demand hits — save money and latency. This taxonomy covers predictive autoscaling in cloud-native and federated cloud-edge environments, mapping future directions. The survey organizes a fragmented field.  The fragmented field finally gets organized properly.
arxiv-2606-07246: High-level synthesis pragmas — compiler hints for hardware — need Pareto-optimal tuning. MailoHLS learns them with multi-adapter structure-aware learning. The learning finds pragmas balancing speed and area. Hardware pragmas need truly intelligent automated tuning. Structure-aware learning balances speed against area.
arxiv-2606-07346: Harmonic representations — decomposing signals into frequencies — can factorize geometrically. This paper develops that geometric factorization for sufficient representations. The factorization reveals the representations' intrinsic shape. Learned representations have intrinsic geometric shape. The factorization reveals that shape very clearly.
arxiv-2606-07446: Dark matter in other galaxies should glow in synchrotron emission — polarized and unpolarized. This paper predicts both from extragalactic targets. The predictions guide radio searches for dark matter. Radio telescopes can hunt for dark matter signals. Synchrotron predictions guide the observations.
arxiv-2606-07546: Short-video recommendation should move beyond item IDs — to semantic-native sequences. This paper scales that modeling. The semantics capture what IDs cannot. Video recommendation is decisively going semantic-native. Traditional item IDs are rapidly becoming obsolete.  Semantic representations capture user intent.
arxiv-2606-07646: Test-time adaptation needs transferable domain variables — learned from sparse supervision. DOME learns them. The variables let models adapt on the fly.  Domain shift plagues deployed machine learning. Learning transferable variables from sparse supervision enables robust test-time adaptation. Robustness improves significantly.
tob-4046:
Plutarch's Morals, the Moralia, collect the essays that stand behind his famous Lives. Written around 100 AD, the essays treat practical philosophy for educated readers: superstition, tranquility of mind, talkativeness, and how a young man should listen to lectures all receive warm, sensible treatment. Plutarch chats where other philosophers lecture.

Vegetarian arguments in On the Eating of Flesh, consolation letters, table talk, and advice on health and marriage broaden the range. Charming and quotable, Plutarch here resembles the ancient world's best advice columnist, learned without heaviness. Readers who know only the biographies will find the essayist equally companionable, and often more personally useful.
tob-0146:
A. P. Sinnett, editor and Theosophist in India, published letters he said came from hidden masters, Morya and Koot Hoomi. The Mahatma Letters, with Blavatsky as the claimed channel, instructed the young movement on the deep structure of things. Followers and skeptics have fought over their origin ever since.

The letters treat cosmic cycles, the afterlife, and the laws that govern adepts and chelas. Sinnett built his books on their teaching. Whether dictated by mahatmas or written nearer home, the letters shaped Theosophy more than any other papers. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10346:
Early Christian Gnostics of the Sethian school treasured the Apocryphon of John, a secret book in which the risen Christ teaches the apostle John. A copy survived among the Nag Hammadi books found in Egypt in 1945. Shorter forms of the same work also survive.

Christ tells how the highest God stands beyond all names, how Sophia fell, and how a lesser maker, Yaldabaoth, built this flawed world with his archons. The account then retells Genesis from that angle. No Gnostic text explains the Sethian system more fully, which is why scholars return to it first.
tob-13146:
Albert G. Mackey, an American physician and leading Masonic scholar, wrote a full History of Freemasonry in the nineteenth century. Mackey's encyclopedia and law books made him the craft's chief American authority. His history long stood as the standard work on the subject.

Mackey traces Masonry from its claimed ancient roots through the medieval building guilds to the modern lodges. He sifts legend from record, explains the degrees and symbols, and defends the order's principles. Masons and historians alike used his volumes for a century, and the work still frames how the fraternity tells its own past.
tob-4146:
Kisari Mohan Ganguli translated the Mahabharata into English prose in the 1880s and 1890s, the first complete rendering of the Sanskrit epic. The Mahabharata, ascribed to the sage Vyasa, is the longest poem in the world. Ganguli worked for over a decade with the support of Indian patrons.

The epic tells of the Bharata princes, the dice game that exiles the Pandavas, and the great war at Kurukshetra that destroys a generation. At its heart stands the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's counsel to Arjuna. Ganguli's plain, full translation carried the whole vast story to English readers and remains the only complete one of its age.
greaves-pyramidographia-1646:
Oxford scholar John Greaves traveled to Egypt and measured the pyramids with care. His Pyramidographia appeared in 1646, among the first English studies of the sites. He brought tools, patience, and a love of exact fact.

Greaves records sizes, passages, and chambers in sober detail. He tests old tales against his own tape and eye. His numbers corrected centuries of loose guessing by travelers. The prose is plain for its age. The book marks a turn: Egypt studied by measure, not just marvel. It remains vital for the history of Egyptology.
huntingdon-witches-examinations-1646:
Huntingdon's accused witches were questioned in 1646, at the crest of the East Anglian hunt led by Matthew Hopkins. The Witches of Huntingdon prints their examinations and confessions in full. The county town saw the panic at its most intense that year.

Confession follows confession in these pages, as the hunt's methods pressed the accused to name themselves and others. Hopkins and his helpers filled gaols across the east with just such work. The pamphlet lets readers judge the words the courts took as proof. It stands as a key record of England's worst witch year.
esdaile-mesmerism-in-india-1846:
James Esdaile cut flesh with no pain in Mesmerism in India, his report of 1846. Esdaile was a Scot healer at a jail ward in India. He found that deep trance, wrought by passes and breath, could dull all pain. Scores of great cuts, some dire, were done while the sick slept calm and woke with no tale of hurt.

He prints each case with care and zeal. Word of his work shook the wards of Britain. Ere sleep drugs came, his proof stood as the best hope of pain free craft. The book is that proof.
askew-examinations-1546:
Anne Askew holds her faith gainst her foes in The Examinations, the record of 1546 and 1547, set here in the Parker Society text of 1849. Askew was a gentlewoman of Lincolnshire whose views broke the king's law on the mass. Chiefs of church and court quizzed her in the Tower. She, a lone dame, matched their wits and gave up no names, e'en when racked past what law let.

John Bale prints her words with hot notes of praise. She was burnt at Smithfield in 1546. The book is her voice, keen and brave, at the stake's edge.
witches-of-huntingdon-1646:
Justices take down witch tales in The Witches of Huntingdon, a brief tract of 1646. In the shire town and its fields, poor folk were charged with pacts with the Devil, who, the tales say, tempts poor souls with coin, food, and ease. The tract prints the quizzes and words of guilt as the justices of the peace took them in the midst of the great war time hunt in the east.

Names, dates, and small grim facts crowd the pages. No scribe shapes them to a tale. The tract is the hunt's raw paper trail. Its plain, prim tone is its worth.
gaule-select-cases-conscience-1646:
John Gaule weighs a priest's doubts in Select Cases of Conscience Touching Witches, his book of 1646. Gaule was a church man in the east, in the midst of the great hunt. Folk brought him hard asks: is my sick bairn bewitched, is my dream a sign, should I shun my next door dame? He replies from the Good Book with care, and with more doubt than the hunt's chiefs liked at that hot hour.

He warns gainst rash claims and cruel tests in plain words. That nerve, in that year, took grit. The book is a rare cool voice from the hunt's own turf.
junius-grand-proces-rothschild-satan-184:
A Paris pamphlet of 1846, signed with the pen name Junius Grand, stages a mock trial in verse and prose. The crowned foe in its title is 'Satan,' named the last king of impostors. The man in the dock is 'Rothschild the First, king of the Jews,' in the pamphlet's own bold words.

The fake trial is a sly hit back at the pamphlet war then raging in Paris. That war made the false tale that the house grew rich on first news of Waterloo. The short piece is a sharp bit of the press fight of its day, kept as a record.
bronte-poems-1846:
Charlotte, Emily, and Anne Brontë published Poems in 1846 as Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell. The slim book was their first publication, paid for with their aunt's legacy money in full. It sold two copies, yet it set three major writers on their road to print.

Charlotte's verses muse on faith, loss, and the life of feeling in a minor key. Emily's poems, the strongest here, sing of the moors, freedom, and a stern inner God. Anne's gentler pieces weigh duty, grief, and hope of heaven with quiet, steady grace in verse. The male pen names hid their sex from a market quick to scorn women's verse then. Critics now prize Emily's lyrics here among the finest short poems of her century.
dumas-chicot-the-jester-1846:
Alexandre Dumas published Chicot the Jester in 1846, as La Dame de Monsoreau in French. The classic abridged English version gives the Valois trilogy's middle volume in one book for readers. Its scene is the court of Henri III, last of the Valois kings of France.

Chicot, the king's jester, is in truth a Gascon noble with a sharp sword and wit. He guards his feckless king against the Guise faction and the League's rising plots in Paris. Bussy d'Amboise loves Diane de Monsoreau, whose husband traps him for a fatal ambush at night. Duels, disguises, and monkish conspiracies crowd the pages at Dumas's swiftest clip of storytelling here. Many readers rank the jester among Dumas's finest and most human creations in fiction.
guizot-civilization-europe-hazlitt-1846:
Francois Guizot's History of Civilization in Europe appears in William Hazlitt's translation of 1846. The book prints Guizot's famous Sorbonne lectures of 1828. Guizot traces European civilization from Rome's fall to the French Revolution. Europe, he argues, grew by the clash and balance of many forces: church, kings, towns, and free thought.

No single power ruled all, and so liberty survived and grew. The lectures made Guizot famous and shaped liberal history across Europe. Hazlitt, son of the essayist, gave the work its English form. The book is the classic liberal account of Europe's rise. Its breadth still impresses students of civilization.
edwards-religious-affections-1746:
Jonathan Edwards preached through the Great Awakening, the revival that swept New England in the 1740s, and saw both its power and its excesses. His Treatise Concerning Religious Affections, published in 1746, asks how to tell true religious experience from false. It is the Awakening's deepest piece of self-examination.

Edwards lists signs that prove nothing: loud emotion, fluent talk, even love of praise disguised as zeal. True grace, he argues, shows in changed practice, humility, and a new taste for the beauty of holy things. Pastors and psychologists of religion still argue with his tests today.
gaule-select-cases-of-conscience-1646:
John Gaule was a Puritan minister who wrote Select Cases of Conscience Touching Witches and Witchcrafts in 1646. He wrote against Matthew Hopkins, the self-styled Witchfinder General whose hunt was then filling English gaols. Gaule's manual is pastoral: it sorts hard cases for troubled consciences.

He distinguishes true witchcraft, as he believed scripture taught it, from melancholy, fraud, and the lies of frightened witnesses. His tests would have acquitted most of the people Hopkins sent to the gallows in those years. The book shows a churchman using his own tradition's tools to slow a witch-hunt.
bonus-margarita-pretiosa-novella-1546:
Petrus Bonus of Ferrara wrote his Margarita Pretiosa Novella, The New Pearl of Great Price, in the 1330s, and printers issued it in 1546. Bonus was a scholastic thinker, trained in the logic of the universities. His book is the great scholastic defense of alchemy's possibility.

He argues that the philosophers' stone is real, that nature ripens metals toward gold, and that the adept's art only speeds her work. His method weighs authorities, answers objections, and builds the case like a disputation in the schools. Later alchemists quoted Bonus as proof that their art had reason on its side.
oliver-historical-landmarks-of-freemason:
George Oliver, an English clergyman and Masonic writer, published Historical Landmarks of Freemasonry in 1846. Oliver studied old lodge records and customs, and he wrote to defend the craft against its critics. His book treats certain rules and customs as fixed landmarks that no Mason may change.

Oliver traced those landmarks through Bible stories, old charges, and lodge tradition, linking modern Masonry to a much older past. He also answered attacks on the order and explained its symbols in moral terms. Readers get both a history and a defense, written by one of the most learned Masonic authors of his century.
darwin-geological-observations-1846:
Charles Darwin's Geological Observations on the Voyage of the Beagle, complete in the 1846 form, gathers his three geology books from the Beagle voyage. Darwin sailed as a young naturalist from 1831 to 1836. His rock work, more than his animal studies, first made his scientific name.

Three parts treat coral reefs, volcanic islands, and the geology of South America. Darwin argued that coral atolls form as volcanic islands slowly sink beneath the sea. He also traced raised beaches and fossils that showed land moving over long ages. Readers see the young Darwin building the deep-time habits of thought that later supported his theory of evolution.
strauss-life-of-jesus-eliot-1846:
David Friedrich Strauss's Life of Jesus Critically Examined appeared in English in 1846, translated by Marian Evans, later George Eliot. The translation was her first book-length work. Strauss, a German theologian, had caused a storm in 1835 by reading the gospel miracles as myth, not history.

Strauss went through the life of Jesus scene by scene, testing each miracle against history and natural law. He argued that early Christians clothed Jesus in the myths their faith expected. German churchmen lost posts over the debate his book began. In English, the translation launched the Victorian crisis of faith, and it pushed its young translator toward the novels that made her famous.
etheridge-syrian-churches-gospels-1846:
John Wesley Etheridge, a Methodist scholar of the Syriac tongue, wrote this 1846 study of the churches of Syria and the east. He paired it with his own literal English version of the four gospels, translated straight from the Peshitta, the Syriac Bible. Longman published the volume in London.

Etheridge traces the Syrian churches, their rites, their writers, and their missions as far as India and China. Then the gospels follow, in wording that often differs in small, telling ways from the Greek-based versions. His aim was to let English readers hear the gospel in a language close to the one Jesus spoke. The book serves both church history and Bible study.
braid-power-of-mind-over-body-1846:
Braid tested Baron Reichenbach's claimed new force in The Power of the Mind over the Body, from 1846. Reichenbach said certain people could see flames from magnets and crystals in the dark. He called the force odic, a new imponderable in nature. Braid's experiments cut the claim down piece by piece.

The sights, he shows, arise from the subject's own mind and body. Expectation and suggestion, not any fluid, produce the marvels. The inquiry marks Braid's turn toward suggestion as the key to trance. It also models how to test a wonder claim fairly. The small book is a classic of skeptical method.
zoist-vol-04-1846:
The Zoist's fourth volume runs from April 1846 to January 1847. Elliotson's journal of mesmerism and cerebral physiology keeps its presses hot. Painless operations under mesmeric trance still headline the case lists. Ether, newly arrived in surgery, begins to shadow the journal's cause in these years.

Reports of clairvoyant somnambulists mix with sober hospital notes. Elliotson defends his methods against a hostile medical establishment. The movement's record grows volume by volume toward thirteen in all. Volume four catches mesmerism at a turning point in its fortunes. Anaesthesia by gas would soon steal its surgical crown. The pages hold the moment before that fall.
plos-pone-0003446:
Yuuki Watanabe and Katsufumi Sato studied how the ocean sunfish swims in this 2008 paper. The sunfish, Mola mola, can weigh up to two tons. It lacks a tail fin and looks like a drifting head. Many people treated it as a slow, plankton-like drifter.

Closer study showed a lift-based swimming style instead. Its tall dorsal and anal fins beat in a symmetric way, like wings. That motion makes the body shape far less odd than it looks. The world's heaviest bony fish turns out to be an active swimmer. Divers had long reported sunfish moving with clear purpose through open water.
plos-pone-0003546:
Stephen Blake and co-authors tracked forest elephants in the Congo Basin for this 2008 study. Road building is expanding fast across that region. The basin holds rich biodiversity, including highly mobile large animals. Forest elephants range widely through dense forest.

Tracking showed roadless wilderness areas determine how elephants move. Roads acted as barriers or channels for their travel. Keeping roadless blocks intact protects elephant corridors. The finding gives planners a direct rule for new road routes. Congo forest elephants are smaller and far more shy than their savanna kin. Their numbers have fallen hard under poaching in recent years of road growth.
plos-pone-0003646:
Sylvie Remaud, Agnès Audibert, and Michel Gho published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Working with the fruit fly Drosophila, they studied the bristle lineage, a set of cells where the Notch signal decides cell fates. They asked when, during the cell cycle, cells answer Notch best.

Using live imaging, the team followed the lineage and switched the Notch pathway on at set times. Cells responded most strongly during S-phase, the stage when a cell copies its DNA. The result shows a cell's readiness to hear a fate signal depends on its own cycle stage.
plos-pone-0003746:
Karl Schmid and Ziheng Yang published this methods critique in PLOS ONE in 2008. Sliding-window analysis is a popular way to scan a protein for signs of natural selection. It compares silent and replacement changes along the sequence, window by window. The authors argue the method has a hidden flaw.

Using the cancer gene BRCA1 as a case, they show how the sliding window can mislead. The trouble lies in how the window treats variation along the protein. The paper urges care with a shortcut many researchers had used on trust when hunting selected regions.
plos-pone-0003846:
David Sevillano, Lorenzo Aguilar, Luis Alou, and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The nasopharynx, the space behind the nose, hosts a normal community of bacteria. Three common species there can also cause respiratory disease. Antibiotics disturb that community's balance.

Using a computerized pharmacodynamic model, the team exposed mixed cultures of the bacteria to beta-lactam antibiotics. They watched how the population dynamics of the whole community shifted. The community view predicts treatment effects on the nasal ecosystem better than testing each germ alone. Germs that share one space do not act as they do alone.
plos-pone-0003946:
Christina T. L. Chen, David I. Gottlieb, and Barak A. Cohen examined DNA near a nerve gene promoter in 2008. Oligodendrocytes are the cells that wrap nerve fibers in myelin. That wrapping speeds nerve signals along the fibers. Loss of myelin plays a part in diseases such as multiple sclerosis.

Their PLOS ONE article focuses on the promoter that controls the Olig2 gene. That promoter holds stretches of DNA kept nearly unchanged across species. Such ultraconserved parts often mark key control switches. Mapping them helps explain how myelin-making cells switch their genes on. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004046:
Shunfu Piao, Sun-Hye Lee, Hyunjoon Kim, and co-authors studied a growth signal switch in 2008. Wnt and beta-catenin signaling guides development across animals. It also plays roles in many diseases when misregulated. Binding of Wnt proteins to the LRP6 coreceptor starts the signal.

Their PLOS ONE article reports how LRP6 shuts down the enzyme GSK3beta. A phosphorylated part of LRP6's inner tail inhibits the enzyme directly. Blocking GSK3beta lets beta-catenin build up and switch genes on. The direct mechanism fills a gap in a widely studied pathway. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004146:
Bronwen Martin and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reproductive capacity and food supply are tightly linked in animals. How an animal adjusts to changes in its surroundings and diet helps decide whether its species endures.

The team measured how changes in dietary energy intake alter gene activity in the gonads, the organs that make eggs and sperm. They tracked which genes switch on or off as food energy rises or falls. The work shows, at the level of genes, how the body senses the reproductive environment and answers with changes in fertility machinery.
plos-pone-0004246:
Zheng Wang and colleagues published this fungal evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fungi that live inside plant leaves, called endophytes, have had a major influence on how reproductive structures evolved in the Leotiomycetes. That group is one of the most problematic in fungal classification, full of disputed relationships.

The team mapped fungal body shapes onto the group's family tree, split into two major lines. They traced how the endophytic lifestyle reshaped the structures fungi use to reproduce. The study uses living arrangements to explain why these fungi look the way they do.
plos-pone-0004346:
Yong Li and Pankaj Agarwal published this disease networks study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human diseases are increasingly seen as not isolated from each other. Understanding how diseases relate through underlying biology could give new insights into their causes, classification, and shared mechanisms. Pathways are the chains of molecular events that carry out a cell's work.

The authors construct a pathway-based view of human diseases and disease relationships. Diseases that share biological pathways are linked, forming a map of illness. Such a map can reveal why some diseases travel together and suggest drugs that might treat several at once.
plos-pone-0004446:
Prion protein sits on cell surfaces doing a job no one fully understands, and Dorothea Rutishauser, Kirsten Mertz, Rita Moos, and co-authors listed its partners in PLOS ONE in 2009. Listing everything a protein touches can reveal what it is for. The team tagged the normal prion protein with a small marker, called a myc tag, near one end.

Mice bred to carry the tagged protein placed it correctly, anchored to the cell surface in the right spots. With the tag as a handle, the team could pull the protein out and name the molecules bound to it. The result is a full native map of its contacts. That map is a starting point for explaining both its normal work and what goes wrong in prion disease.
plos-pone-0004546:
A heat shock protein helps a small insect repair the damage of winter cold, show Vladimir Kostal and Michaela Tollarova-Borovanska in PLOS ONE in 2009. The insect is Pyrrhocoris apterus, a red firebug. Adults that pass winter in a dormant state, called diapause, tolerate cold very well. Adults that keep reproducing lack the full set of cold-tolerance adaptations and survive cold poorly.

The protein is the 70 kilodalton heat shock protein, a general cell repair helper despite its name. The authors show it assists during repair of chilling injury in this insect. Studying how insects fix cold damage helps explain who survives winter and where species can live. It also informs the storage of insects used in research and farming.
plos-pone-0004646:
People, not wind or water, carry a tree-killing nematode across China, show Christelle Robinet, Alain Roques, Hongyang Pan, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The pinewood nematode is a microscopic worm that kills pine trees. Intensification of world trade is responsible for an increase in alien species introductions. Human-mediated dispersal promotes not only introductions but also expansion of a species' range through long-distance jumps.

The team modeled the nematode's spread in China, separating natural dispersal from human-carried movement. Their conclusion, in the title, is that human-mediated dispersal plays the key role. That finding directs control efforts at timber transport and trade routes. Stopping the trucks and shipments matters more than fencing forests against a worm that barely travels on its own.
plos-pone-0004746:
Eileen Kennedy and colleagues found distant spots in an enzyme that tune its activity without touching the active site, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Far apart parts of an enzyme must talk to each other for control to work. Finding the parts in those talks has been hard, since the contacts are weak and subtle.

Protein kinases, which add phosphate tags to other proteins, are a prime case. The team hunted for non cutting residues that still shift kinase action. Such spots could be new drug targets that tune, rather than block, the enzyme. That may mean fewer side effects.
kennan-long-telegram-1946:
George Kennan, an American diplomat in Moscow, sent the Long Telegram to Washington in February 1946. The cable ran to some 8,000 words, far longer than normal diplomatic traffic. Officials had asked why the Soviet Union opposed a Western-led world bank, and Kennan answered with a full account of Soviet thinking.

He described a regime that felt insecure, pushed outward by ideology and habit, yet moved with patience rather than fixed plans. Against such a rival, he argued, the United States needed firm and patient resistance at every point. The telegram spread through the government at once and gave shape to the policy soon named containment, which guided American strategy for the Cold War.
cia-0000008146:
Brazil under President Joao Goulart gets a short-term forecast in a CIA paper from November 1961. Goulart had taken office weeks earlier, after the previous president suddenly resigned. Conservatives, the military, and Washington all doubted the left-leaning new leader.

The paper weighs inflation, unrest, and the armed forces' mood over the near term. Its judgments belong to the road that led to Brazil's 1964 coup. Readers can watch analysts mark warning signs while outcomes were still in doubt. Country forecasts like this one were the quiet routine of Cold War intelligence, filed country by country.
cia-0000008746:
Near Bac Giang city, in the Vong Xe area, an American pilot was sighted according to a January 1973 CIA report. The area falls in Ha Bac province, northeast of Hanoi. Reports from this month arrived just before the Paris accords ended American combat.

A pilot seen on the ground could be evading, captured, or already dead, and the file had to be read with care. Officials matched such sightings to the day's loss lists. When no match came, the report stayed open as a lead. This entry preserves one lead from the war's closing weeks.
cia-0000009446:
One American and about one hundred Vietnamese prisoners were sighted in Laos in an April 1972 report, on a journey the title cuts short. The imbalance in the numbers is itself the story: captivity in Laos fell mostly on Asians. Prisoners were often moved on foot between camps.

A moving column offered witnesses a rare open view of the prison system. Analysts could estimate camp populations from such counts and sightings. The lone American in the column gained a dated place in his file. The report preserves that sighting, and the larger human column around him, in one frame.
cia-0000011346:
In February 1964 the CIA surveyed the outlook for North Vietnam, covering its internal politics, its political problems, and its economy. The paper came just months before the Gulf of Tonkin clash pulled the United States deep into the Vietnam War. Hanoi's communist government was backing the revolt in the south while bracing for American power.

Analysts probed how Hanoi's leaders thought, what they aimed for, and how their state was holding up. The study tries to read an enemy capital that Washington understood poorly. It stands as a record of American knowledge on the eve of a long and costly escalation.
cia-0000011646:
Ukraine's fate in the war between Germany and the Soviet Union is the subject of a CIA paper from January 1949. Ukraine had been fought over, occupied, and starved during the war, and millions of its people were dead or displaced. The young agency studied the question as the Cold War froze Europe into two camps.

The paper weighs Ukrainian resistance to Soviet rule and the politics of the displaced people scattered after the war. It treats Ukraine as a nation held inside the Soviet Union against the will of many of its people. The study shows how early Washington looked for cracks behind the Iron Curtain.
cia-0000011846:
Months before elections in the Dominican Republic, a CIA paper from March 1966 weighs the island's prospects for stability. The American intervention of 1965 had put down the civil war and installed a provisional order. Joaquín Balaguer, the old strongman's heir, was preparing the comeback that would win him the presidency that year.

The paper judges the new order's chances against the country's old divisions. It weighs the parties, the military, and the habits of strongman rule that died hard. The study shows analysts doubting the calm even as they recorded it, in a country Washington had just occupied.
cia-0000012246:
Crisis was gathering over Indonesia in June 1964, and a CIA paper that month weighs the archipelago's prospects. The communist party, the PKI, was growing fast under Sukarno's protection. The army watched and waited, its patience thinning, while the economy slid and the Confrontation with Malaysia drained the state.

The paper judges how the balance among Sukarno, the army, and the communists might break. It weighs the chances of a showdown and what might follow one. Written the year before a bloodbath killed hundreds of thousands, it shows the storm's shape forming, unnamed, on the horizon.
cia-0000012346:
Support is the quoted word that survives in a Helms memo to the CIA director from March 1962. Its full subject, a Military Thought matter, is cut short in the file's title. Another veiled page thus joins the summit file: the substance hides behind truncation, while the significance shows in the letterhead and the names it joins.

Guarded memoranda like this one carried the important things that could not be said openly. The file keeps them in sequence with the plainer papers. For readers, the memo marks how much of the era's greatest case still moves behind black bars.
cia-0000013246:
A change in food ration policy toward prisoners of war is noted in a CIA item from November 1967. Even the prisoners' rice bowls were policy instruments in the camps. Rations rose or fell with orders from above, with the harvest, and with the captors' wish to reward, punish, or display their charges. A note on rations is, in truth, a note on life and death at the slowest scale.

The item tracks the change and its meaning for the men held. Small entries like this fed the great accounting's picture of conditions. For readers, it is logistical detail with a human weight: the bowls, measured.
cia-0000013846: A CIA note dated April 2, 1967, carries only a short title: Captured US POW. No place or unit is named in the title itself. The note still mattered, since each capture report fed the wider count of Americans held in Vietnam. Even the bare records helped officials track who was missing and where prisoners were last seen.
cia-0000014746: Gerard Piel, also written as Jerry Piel, is the subject of a CIA file dated November 4, 1967. Piel was a noted science publisher in those years. Why a publisher drew a file, the title does not say. Name files of this kind mark the wide net the agency cast over public life.
cia-0000015346: FCC monitoring and flying saucers meet in a CIA file dated November 2, 1952. The FCC watched the airwaves, where saucer tales spread by radio. Broadcast claims could stir crowds faster than print. A file joining the two shows officials tracking the story's spread, not just the sightings in the sky. The FCC file now sits in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015446: Flying saucers seen over Sweden are the subject of a CIA record dated February 5, 1959. Sweden produced steady sighting reports through the nineteen fifties, and this entry adds one more. The title names no town, witness, or shape, so the description stays at that level. What it shows is reach: a report from Scandinavia was read and filed in Washington.
cia-0000022246: Identity cards of captured American pilots were shown on television, a CIA record dated November 4, 1967, reports. The same title notes an appeal by AALAPSO for thirty seven of something the catalog cuts off. Showing ID cards proved captures to the world. It also handed watchers names and faces that could be matched against the lists of missing airmen.
cia-0000027646: Probable consequences of the forthcoming West German elections are weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1949. The vote that year founded the Federal Republic and made Adenauer its first chancellor. Judging consequences before a first election meant guessing a whole country's direction. The paper stands at the birth of the West German state that anchored Europe for forty years.
cia-0000036846:
A Pravda dispatch titled Missiles in the Air, by Shoephov, is noted in a CIA record dated November 5, 1967. Pravda was the Soviet Communist Party's main newspaper. The item reached the file through a review of what the Soviet press was saying.

The dispatch deals with missiles and air power, themes at the heart of the Cold War arms race. American readers of Pravda looked for signals about Soviet aims and claims. The file shows how even a single newspaper piece was clipped, translated, and kept on record. Soviet papers were read in Washington almost as closely as they were read in Moscow itself.
cia-0000038946: The United States Vietnam Mission and its domestic service in Vietnamese are the subject of a CIA record dated March 1, 1970. The title notes the service as of April 16, in a year the catalog entry leaves unstated. The record concerns broadcasting or information work aimed at a Vietnamese audience at home. Little else can be grounded from the title alone. The file is best read as a small piece of the mission's daily information work in wartime Saigon.
cia-0000042346:
Soviet media reported a multitude of UFO sightings, in a CIA record dated October 3, 1989. The late Soviet press was newly open under glasnost. Stories once kept out of print now reached Soviet readers in large numbers.

Inside, the record gathers the wave of sighting reports from Soviet outlets. American readers tracked Soviet media for far more than flying saucers. An open press was itself the bigger story of 1989. Soviet readers were suddenly free to read about almost anything their editors chose to print. The saucer reports showed, in a curious form, how much the old controls on Soviet news had loosened by that autumn.
cia-0000045246:
The armed forces backed Duarte on the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. An army's public backing steadied a president under personal attack. It also reminded everyone where the guns in the argument lived.

Inside, the military's support for its commander in chief is recorded. Such backing was not automatic in El Salvador's strained politics. The army and the president had quarreled before over how the war should be fought. Generals had their own view of talks with the guerrillas. The file preserves the moment they closed ranks behind Duarte anyway, a show of unity that held the state together while the crisis ran its course.
cia-0000046646: General John Vessey's planned trip to Vietnam hung in doubt in the spring of 1987, and a CIA item dated March 1, 1987, records the uncertainty. A second envoy's visit, by Richard Childress, was reported as not considered at all. Vessey was Washington's senior envoy on the missing-men issue, so his travel plans carried real diplomatic weight.
cia-0000049046: An alleged massacre of civilians in Sonsonate Department by members of the armed forces fills a CIA item from 1983. Sonsonate lies in western El Salvador, coffee country that saw steady war. Allegations of this kind reached the files by the hundred; the Truth Commission's work was to sort the provable from the rest.
cia-0000049246:
A CIA study from 1988 examines the FMLN, the guerrilla front fighting El Salvador's government. Its subject is double: the front's strategy in negotiations, and its human rights abuses. By 1988 the war was a stalemate, and both sides were testing whether talks could do what battles had not. The study belongs to the war's analytic record.

Inside, the front's bargaining is weighed beside its conduct: how it talked, what it demanded, and how its forces treated the people under their guns. Pairing the two subjects was the analysts' point, since a movement's record at the table and in the field shaped each other. The study shows Washington reading the rebels as a government in waiting, flaws counted.
cia-0000095146: Comment on certain questions relating to the situation in Laos is the title of declassified CIA document 0000095146, dated May 6, 1964. The heading is cautious and general, naming Laos and questions rather than answers. Readers find a short declassified comment item whose vagueness is worth noting, since the record promises questions about a situation, not findings.
cia-0000096946: Opening statement regarding CIA involvement with ITT Chile is declassified CIA document 0000096946, dated January 3, 1973. The heading frames the text as an opening statement on that involvement. The brief file begins a small cluster of Chile and ITT records, preserved as formal testimony material rather than field reporting from the agency's files.
cia-0000102946: Use of Forced Labor in Mining, Railroad and Construction Enterprises, plus locations in cut-short form, is declassified CIA document 0000102946, dated September 3, 1983. Three industries share the heading. Readers find a short multi-industry labor record, broader than the single-project items, filed as the cluster's coverage of forced labor reaches its widest spread.

plos-pone-0004846:
Cherie Bond, Martina Zimmermann, and Susan Greenfield studied upregulation of alpha7 nicotinic receptors by acetylcholinesterase C-terminal peptides, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The alpha7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a potent calcium ionophore implicated in excitotoxicity and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer disease. Previous research implicated fragments of the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in modulating receptor levels in brain cells.

Peptide exposure increased receptor numbers. More receptors may amplify calcium damage. Or compensation may protect neurons under stress. The pathway links two classic Alzheimer players. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0005446:
Monica Ardura and colleagues studied children with severe staph infections in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Staphylococcus aureus can cause deep and dangerous illness in children who were healthy before. Much is known about the germ itself, but less about how a child's immune system answers it.

The team compared blood immune cells from sick children with those from healthy children. One group of defender cells reacted more strongly than usual in the sick children. At the same time, memory T cells in the blood were lower. Those shifts may help explain why the infection hits some children so hard.
plos-pone-0005546:
Changhai Tian, L Charles Murrin, and Jialin Zheng studied methamphetamine harm in young rat brain cells, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The drug methamphetamine can damage the ends of dopamine nerve cells and kill cells in movement areas of the brain. Harm was thought to run through stress pathways linking cell compartments.

The team looked at early nerve cells in the hippocampus, the brain's memory centre. They linked breaking apart of the cells' energy centres to the death of those young cells. That widens the known reach of the drug's harm in the brain.
plos-pone-0005646:
Emelyn Shroff and co-authors studied peptides that trigger cell death in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A family of proteins governs whether a cell lives or dies by suicide. Small members of the family, the BH3-only proteins, start the death process by binding the family's survival members.

The team used short peptides copied from those death domains. The peptides made mitochondria split apart and cells die, even without two proteins long thought essential for death. That surprise opens a new angle on how death can be triggered in cancer cells. Mitochondrial splitting is a normal event as well, so the death route the peptides open needs more mapping.
plos-pone-0005746:
S. Ivan Perez and co-authors compared skull shapes and DNA in early Americans in 2009, and found the two records at odds. How many founding groups peopled the Americas is a long-running debate. Skulls from the Holocene vary in ways some read as signs of two distinct source groups.

Gene data, the team notes, point more toward a single shared origin. They weigh why bones and genes might tell different tales, from diet-driven skull change to drift. The clash warns against reading ancestry from one kind of evidence alone. Both records must be explained by any sound history of the first Americans.
plos-pone-0005846:
Wolfgang Wagner and co-authors compared aging in the body with aging in a dish in 2009. Stem and progenitor cells lose power with age, limiting repair. Cells grown in culture also age, enlarging and stopping division after many rounds, a state called replicative senescence.

The team found the two kinds of aging leave related marks on human stem cells. Shared marks suggest culture aging is a fair, faster model of real aging for some questions. That matters because body aging takes decades to study. The shared signature also names candidate drivers of stem cell decline that drugs might target.
plos-pone-0006446:
Geoffry De Iuliis and colleagues tested mobile phone radiation on human sperm in the lab, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Whether such radiation harms human health has been much debated. Male reproduction is a key part of that debate, since some studies link phone use with poorer sperm. The team exposed sperm samples outside the body to phone-type radiation.

Their title states the outcome: the radiation raised reactive oxygen species and caused DNA damage in the sperm. Results in a dish cannot settle what happens in daily life. Still, the study adds hard lab data to a heated public question. It also suggests paths for follow-up work.
plos-pone-0006546:
Jenny Gunnersen and colleagues studied a seizure-related gene in the eye for PLOS ONE in 2009. Seizure-related gene 6, or Sez-6, is expressed in neurons of the mouse brain, retina, and spinal cord. In the cortex it helps specify dendritic branching patterns. The team examined Sez-6 in amacrine cells of the rodent retina.

They also studied the consequence of deleting the gene. Retinal amacrine cells shape how visual signals are processed before leaving the eye. A gene that patterns their branches could affect vision itself. The study links a brain gene to the wiring of the retina.
plos-pone-0006646:
Marijana Radonjic and co-authors read liver gene activity under high-fat diets in PLOS ONE in 2009. Excessive exposure to dietary fats is an important factor in initiation of obesity and metabolic syndrome pathologies. The cellular processes associated with adaptation were their focus. They ran genome-wide mRNA expression analysis of hepatic adaptation to high-fat diets.

Their title reports a switch from an inflammatory to a metabolic program over time. The liver's response evolves rather than staying fixed. Timing therefore matters when interpreting diet studies. A staged response suggests different interventions for early versus late disease.
plos-pone-0009446:
Claudia Miranda and colleagues examined a cancer linked protein pair in PLOS ONE in 2010. TRK proteins are changed forms of a growth receptor. When stuck in the on state, they can turn normal cells cancer like. A relay protein named STAT3 is switched on when TRK is active. The team tested what STAT3 does in that change.

Working with cells in the lab, they probed whether STAT3 is needed for TRK driven change. Their results place STAT3 inside the chain of signals that TRK uses. Knowing that chain in detail points to steps that drugs might block. It adds to the map of how these rare growth receptors cause cancer.
plos-pone-0009546:
Thierry Lefevre and colleagues tested a link between beer and mosquito bites in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria spreads when mosquitoes bite people. Drinking alcohol is rising in many lands where malaria is common. The team asked whether drinking beer changes how many mosquitoes seek a person. Volunteers drank beer or water, and the air around them was offered to mosquitoes.

Mosquitoes chose the air of beer drinkers more often. Something in breath or skin odor after drinking draws them in. The result joins two public health problems in an unexpected way. Advice on malaria prevention may need to reckon with drinking as a risk factor.
plos-pone-0009646:
Kiran Mahajan and co-authors pinpointed a switch on a growth protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. AKT is a central driver of cell growth and survival. It is switched on by chemical tags at specific spots. The team showed that an enzyme called Ack1 tags AKT at one spot, tyrosine 176. That tag had not been recognized as a key control before.

Tagging at that spot proved to regulate how AKT is activated. A precise switch in a cancer relevant pathway is valuable knowledge. Drugs could aim at the tagging step rather than at AKT itself. The study gives drug designers an exact molecular address to consider.
plos-pone-0010446:
Geneviève Mailhot and colleagues linked a cystic fibrosis protein to fat handling in gut cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. People with cystic fibrosis often show abnormal fat patterns in blood and tissues. Even carriers of one faulty gene copy can show them. The faulty protein, CFTR, is best known as a channel in airways and gut. Why its loss distorts fats was poorly understood.

Using a human gut cell line, the team lowered CFTR and watched fats change. Fat composition shifted, and fat-making activity rose. A channel protein thus influences fat chemistry more broadly than expected. That link may explain digestive troubles that burden patients daily. It could also suggest dietary or drug corrections worth testing.
plos-pone-0010546:
Michael Widmann, Peter Trodler and Jürgen Pleiss carried out a systematic study of the near-neutral zone of proteins in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proteins carry electric charge that changes with acidity. Near a certain acidity, their net charge falls almost to zero; that band is the isoelectric region. It predicts how proteins bind in ion exchange columns, a workhorse purification method. Labs tune acidity and salt to exploit that binding.

A systematic map of the region helps chemists plan purifications instead of guessing. Predicting binding saves costly trial and error on valuable samples. The study treats a routine lab step with unusual rigor. Protein purification underlies most drug and enzyme research. Better prediction there quietly speeds many other projects.
plos-pone-0010646:
Jeshmi Jeyabalan and colleagues studied a small protein tied to a rare bone disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, SEDLIN, helps move cargo inside cells. Changes in its gene cause a childhood disorder that distorts growing joints and spine.

The team showed SEDLIN pairs with an identical copy of itself. They also mapped how disease-causing changes affect its contacts with three gene-control proteins. Some mutants kept the pairing but lost other contacts. Separating those effects helps explain why similar mutations can cause quite different severity in different patients.
plos-pone-0010746:
Chirag Patel, Jayanta Bhattacharya, and Atul Butte scanned many environmental factors for links to type 2 diabetes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diabetes arises from genes mixed with surroundings and habits. Genome scans test thousands of gene variants at once; no matching scan existed for exposures.

Their pilot scan tested hundreds of measurable exposures against diabetes in survey data. A few strong links stood out, including some pollutants. Many weaker links were likely noise, and the authors say so plainly. The study's value is the method: a wide, even-handed screen that other diseases can now borrow.
plos-pone-0010846:
Ashkan Emadi, Ashley Ross, Kathleen Cowan and co-authors published this drug study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They worked with dimeric naphthoquinones, twin-ring compounds first made to block an HIV enzyme but later found to kill leukemia cells by an unknown route. To learn how these compounds act, the team turned to yeast.

They screened a library of yeast strains, each missing a single gene, for strains that grew better or worse when exposed to the compounds. Strains lacking genes for mitochondria, the cell's power plants, and for respiration were extra sensitive. Follow-up tests pointed the same way, toward energy production inside the cell. Emadi and colleagues use a simple organism to map a drug's weak spots, a strategy that can guide the design of new cancer compounds.
plos-pone-0010946:
Akihide Takeuchi, Motoyasu Hosokawa, Takayuki Nojima and co-authors published this splicing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells build different proteins in different tissues by alternative splicing, cutting and rejoining a gene's message in varied ways. The hardest case is mutually exclusive exons, where exactly one of several segments must be picked, and how the cell guarantees a clean either-or choice was unclear.

The authors built reporter mice whose tissues glow one color or another depending on which exon gets chosen, making the switch visible across the body. Tracking that signal revealed a conserved switching mechanism rather than a loose balance of competing factors. Takeuchi and colleagues supply a living readout for the splice code. Such tools help explain how tissues get their distinct protein sets, and how splicing errors cause disease.
plos-pone-0011046:
Tristan Hedrick and Jack Waters published this brain cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The nucleus basalis, at the back of the basal forebrain, supplies the cortex with acetylcholine, a chemical central to arousal and attention, and it degenerates in Alzheimer's disease. Its large neurons had never been characterized electrically, unlike their counterparts in neighboring regions, so the authors recorded from them in mouse brain slices.

They patched onto magnocellular neurons from young adult mice, then stained each recorded cell afterward to learn whether it was cholinergic or not. Comparing the two classes revealed how their firing patterns, inputs, and resting behavior differ. Hedrick and Waters supply the basic electrical profile of a nucleus that attention research and dementia studies both depend on, a reference that future work on its decline will need.
plos-pone-0011146:
Krankel, Armstrong, McArdle and colleagues examined young diabetic patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. Even before heart disease appears, type 1 diabetes may harm the blood's repair cells. The team tested how blood cells that support vessels respond to kinin, a signal that normally aids repair.

Responses to kinin were altered in cells from young patients, showing early wear on the repair system. Catching vessel harm this early argues for action long before symptoms start. If repair can be restored, later heart disease might be delayed or prevented. The study gives a cell level reason to treat young patients proactively.
plos-pone-0011246:
Priest, Bereknyei, Hooper and colleagues observed hospital rounds in PLOS ONE in 2010. On rounds, medical teams visit patients, discuss cases and teach students. The team recorded where rounds happened and what was discussed, then related both to specialty, hospital, patient load and team size.

Setting and content varied in clear patterns with those factors. Bedside rounds differ from hallway or conference room rounds in what gets covered. That matters for training, since students learn medicine largely on rounds. Hospitals can use such evidence to plan rounds that teach better and include patients more fully.
plos-pone-0011346:
Kathleen Schwerdtner Máñez and Sebastian Ferse traced the history of trepang fishing in their 2010 paper. Trepang is sea cucumber, dried and sold as a prized food and trade good in Asian markets. For centuries, sailors from Makassar, on the island of Sulawesi, sailed north to fish trepang along distant coasts, including northern Australia.

Their account follows how the fishery grew, how trade routes linked Makassar with buyers in China, and how contact with Aboriginal Australians shaped the voyages. The fishery is one of the oldest sustained links between Australia and Asia, long before European settlement. Reading that history restores credit to Indigenous and Makassan seafarers. It also shows how one marine product could bind together economies and cultures across a wide sea.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1246:
The President wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 24 July 1945. Truman's word reached the China post from the middle of the German talks. A presidential message steadied an envoy's hand like nothing else in the service.

Hurley's task in China was delicate: back the Nationalist government, press it toward unity with its communist rivals, and keep China in the war. Orders from the top set the line for that work. This note is the commander in chief tending the far end of his alliance. It shows the summit's leader ruling by cable across two oceans at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1346:
Clement Attlee wrote to President Truman on 31 July 1945, days after becoming prime minister of Britain. Attlee had beaten Churchill at the polls and taken his seat at the Potsdam table mid-conference. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Few letters in the volume carry a change of government inside them. Attlee's note opens the working tie between the new Labour government in London and Truman's White House. It also marks the strange shape of Potsdam, where one of the three delegations changed its leader halfway through. Readers can see the new prime minister step into the talks in his own words.
frus-1945-50-intel-d46:
A paper prepared for the Secretary of State's Staff Committee is dated 15 November 1945. The staff committee was where the department's senior men settled questions for the secretary. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Papers written for a committee are drafted to be argued over, so they often state the options with unusual clarity. This one fed the State Department's top table as the intelligence contest moved toward decision. Readers can use it to see how the department framed the choice for itself, apart from what it told rivals. The distinction matters: what an agency says in its own room is the truest map of what it wants and what it fears.
frus-1945-50-intel-d146:
On 8 April 1946 the Third Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The State Department prints it as document 146 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

The text is the meeting as the secretaries kept it, topic by topic, with the results marked as they were reached. Such pages are often the only proof of when a choice was made, and by whom. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d246:
Dated 3 November 1947, this memorandum runs from the Assistant Executive Secretary (Lay) to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The Office of the Historian kept it as document 246 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d346:
A memorandum dated 4 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. The State Department prints it as document 346 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1861-d46:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 21 May 1861. The letter is document 46 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The letter of 21 May became famous for its harsh tone toward Britain. Lincoln and Seward softened its sharpest lines before it went out. Even so, it warned London plainly against any step that aided the South. Few single letters in the volume carry such weight in the history of the war. Lincoln's edit of the letter is one of the great acts of his early war leadership.
frus-1861-d146:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 August 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 146 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Same day writing on both ends of the Paris line was by now a habit of the record. Dayton's page reports the view from the Seine as Seward's sets the line from the Potomac. The file's strength is this doubled view of one tie. The doubled view is what makes this printed record so rich for readers now. A doubled view of one tie gives this record its rare, stereo depth.
frus-1861-d246:
In a letter dated 26 July 1861, William H. Seward gave James Shepherd Pike his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 246 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d46:
News and judgment from Charles Francis Adams reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 11 April 1862. It was printed as Document 46 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d146:
On 17 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch from Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is printed as Document 146 in the Foreign Relations volume that the State Department laid before Congress with the President's yearly message.

That same day, Union and Confederate armies fought at Antietam in Maryland, the bloodiest single day of the Civil War. News crossed the Atlantic by ship, so London learned of battles days after Washington did. Dispatches from this week show the lag built into wartime statecraft, and the care both men took with news that could sway British policy.
frus-1862-d246:
On 26 December 1861 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, in a dispatch printed as Document 246 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was Seward's first Paris letter in this file.

Boxing Day 1861 was also the day Washington decided to free the envoys seized from the Trent, ending the crisis with Britain. Seward wrote to Paris as that settlement took shape. His letters to Dayton through the next year pressed one point. France should leave the American war alone and expect no Union blessing for adventures elsewhere. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d346:
Filed out of order as Document 346, a Dayton report dated 6 November 1862 went from Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. William L. Dayton was the American minister to France.

Dayton wrote two days after the Northern elections and in the week of the British cabinet's decision on the truce plan. His report thus sits at the crossing of the war's political and diplomatic threads. In the printed file it arrives late, among mid-November papers, a placement the reader must correct by its date. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d446:
On 17 February 1862 Norman B. Judd reported from Berlin to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 446 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Judd's February report came as Union forces took Fort Donelson and opened the Tennessee River, victories that strengthened the Union's name in Europe. In Berlin he watched a Prussia busy with its own army reforms and its rivalry with Austria. His letters told Washington how the German world weighed the American war. For readers, the Berlin file is a useful contrast to London and Paris. At this court the Union's task was to keep goodwill warm. It did not have to head off harm.
frus-1862-d546:
Roest van Limburg received this reply from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 September 1862. The note is Document 546 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Seward's mid-September notes to resident ministers were written in the shadow of the Maryland campaign, four days before Antietam. His Dutch reply handled the standing business between the governments with the Department's usual exactness. For Van Limburg, a written American answer was the useful thing: it could be sent home to The Hague as the Union's stated position. The exchange illustrates why both sides valued this formal traffic. It fixed positions, prevented surprise, and kept a useful friendship in repair during the war's most anxious fortnight.
frus-1862-d646:
On 30 April 1862, Robert H. Pruyn wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Pruyn was the new American minister to Japan, picked to take over the legation from Townsend Harris. His dispatch appears as document 646 in the Foreign Relations volume that covers 1862.

A new envoy's early letters told Washington what he found on taking up his post. Pruyn's report belongs to the hand-over between the first American mission to Japan and the men who would run it through the Civil War years. It is a plain, working piece of the record that tied a far-off legation to the State Department.
frus-1863p1-d46:
On 28 October 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote again to James M. Mason, the South's envoy in London. Benjamin headed the Confederate state office in Richmond. The letter is document 46 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A month had passed since Benjamin's last letter to Mason in this file, and the ground had shifted. Antietam was fought, and the freedom edict was on its way. Letters from Richmond had to keep envoys' hopes up as the facts grew hard. This one is part of that strain. Kept in the Union's printed record, it shows the South's London brief run from Richmond, sheet by sheet.
frus-1863p1-d146:
On 7 April 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. A dispatch from Adams bears the same date in the volume. The letter is document 146 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote in the same week Adams reported on the seized raider, though neither man yet had the other's sheet. The cross of dates is the sea mail at work. His letter fed the brief at a bright point: Britain had at last held a Southern ship. This one is Washington's half of the day's exchange, set beside London's in the printed file.
frus-1863p1-d246:
Reporting on 23 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 246 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d346:
Writing in Washington on 31 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 346 in the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons knew that harsh words could push the two nations toward a fight neither wanted. His notes are firm on British rights but measured in tone. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war. Each side kept copies of the whole exchange, which is why the printed volume can show the argument from both desks.
frus-1863p1-d446:
The date 4 April 1863 heads a letter from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d546:
Writing on 1 June 1863, Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward addressed Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington in an official letter. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the early summer of 1863. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d646:
Dated 23 October 1863, document 646 is a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
plos-pbio-0020246:
Christopher K. Patil, Hao Li, and Peter Walter studied stress gene control in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. When proteins misfold in the cell's folding compartment, the unfolded protein response switches on rescue genes. A protein called Gcn4p is one of the switches, and the team found new DNA sites that help it work.

Those sites sit upstream of the rescue genes, where switches bind. Finding them explains how Gcn4p picks its targets. The study adds detail to one of the best-known stress circuits in biology. The same circuit is active in human diseases from diabetes to cancer. Each new control point is a chance to understand the response, and perhaps tune it.
plos-pone-0000146:
Sanja Glisic-Milosavljevic, Jill Waukau, Parthav Jailwala, and colleagues published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It looks at people at risk for type 1 diabetes and people who had just developed it. The team focused on a group of immune cells, the CD4+CD25+ high T-cell fraction, which helps keep the immune system in balance.

The authors report more apoptosis, programmed cell death, in that cell group among the at-risk and recent-onset subjects. Losing these peacekeeper cells could help explain how the immune attack on the pancreas gets started. The finding adds a clue to the early events of type 1 diabetes, before symptoms appear.
plos-pone-0000246:
Eva Schönenberger, Dirk Schnapauff, Florian Teige, and colleagues published this patient study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Coronary angiography pictures the heart's arteries, either noninvasively by scan or invasively by catheter. The authors measure patient acceptance of both forms, asking which patients prefer and why.

A test only helps if patients agree to take it. The study compares comfort, worry, and willingness between the scan and the catheter procedure. Its findings guide cardiology services choosing which test to offer first, balancing picture quality against the patient experience. Those answers give clinics firm ground for planning their services.
plos-pone-0000346:
Silvia Landi, Maria Cristina Cenni, Lamberto Maffei, and colleagues published this visual development study in PLOS ONE in 2007. An enriched environment, full of stimulation, speeds the development of the visual system. The authors study retinal ganglion cells, whose branching patterns, dendritic stratification, develop under that enrichment. They show the effect requires retinal BDNF, a growth factor in the eye itself.
