The brain's response to a rich environment was known; this paper locates part of the mechanism in the retina. BDNF in the eye proves necessary for the enrichment effect on cell branching. The work connects upbringing conditions to molecular events at the very first stage of vision.
plos-pone-0000446:
Alex Kentsis and colleagues calculated the energetics of a protein folding, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. A protein's chain must fold into one precise shape to work, and the free energy of folding measures how stable that shape is. The team also calculated cooperativity, the tendency of folding to happen all at once rather than in pieces.

Accurate energy calculations test whether physical theory truly explains folding, biology's classic puzzle. Cooperativity matters because an all-or-nothing fold is less likely to get stuck in harmful half-folded states, which are linked to diseases like Alzheimer's. Computational studies of this kind benchmark the methods that drug designers also rely on.
plos-pone-0000546:
Marcus A. Gray and colleagues tricked volunteers' brains with false body signals and watched emotion change, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Participants in an fMRI scanner received false physiological feedback, misleading information about their own heart rate, while judging emotional material. The team measured the modulation of emotional appraisal by that feedback.

How people feel depends partly on what they believe their body is doing. Fake feedback that shifts appraisal shows emotion is partly an interpretation, not just a reaction. Brain imaging reveals where that interpretation happens, informing theories of anxiety, where body signals are often misread.
plos-pone-0000646:
Tatyana Sharpee and William Bialek wrote a theory study on how neurons sort signals, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. A neuron faces signals with many dimensions, yet its output is often binary: fire or not. The authors ask how to draw the boundary between two signal categories so the yes-or-no answer carries the most possible information.

Their motivation comes straight from the nervous system, which must squeeze rich inputs through single spikes. The math of maximal information transmission sets what the best boundary looks like. Work like this guides experiments on real neurons, and it also informs the design of artificial systems that must classify signals with limited output.
plos-pone-0000746:
Jia-Ching Shieh, Yu-Che Cheng, Mao-Chang Su and colleagues built designer gene switches and put them to work in yeast. Zinc fingers are DNA-binding motifs that can distinguish different DNA sequences, making them suitable for engineering artificial transcription factors. Their test bed was the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, genetics' favorite test kitchen, and their target gene was FLO11.

The tailor-made factors switched FLO11 on, with visible phenotypic consequences for the yeast. A gene like FLO11 changes how yeast cells stick and spread, so flipping it shows the switches truly govern traits. Success in yeast is a step toward programmable gene control in medicine and industry.
plos-pone-0000846:
Simon L. Zeller, Helmut Brandl and Bernhard Schmid studied whether soil bacteria pick their plant partners, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Belowground microorganisms influence plant performance by altering the soil environment. Plant pathogens such as cyanide-producing strains of the rhizobacterium Pseudomonas may show strong host-plant selectivity, harming some species while sparing others. The team analyzed interactions between different host plants and these bacteria.

Their model system pairs a crop with a weed, the pairing that decides farm yields. If rhizobacteria suppress the weed more than the crop, microbes become allies in weed control. If they hit the crop, they are hidden pests. Selectivity data tell farmers which story their soils are telling.
plos-pone-0000946:
Ying Sheng, Par Engstrom and Boris Lenhard built a computer model to predict microRNA genes in mammals, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces, about twenty-two letters long, that tune gene activity. They can order a message destroyed or block its use, so finding them matters.

Hundreds were already known in mouse and human, but more were surely missed. The authors train a support vector machine, a pattern learning program, on both sequence and folded shape. Shape matters because microRNAs form a distinct hairpin. A better predictor hands biologists a fuller parts list for gene control.
plos-pone-0001046:
Teresa Treweek, Heath Ecroyd, Danielle Williams and colleagues tuned a chaperone protein and watched its protection change, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Amyloid fibrils, ordered protein clumps, mark Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and prion diseases. Chaperones such as alphaB-crystallin help stop proteins from depositing that way.

The team made site directed changes in the protein's tail extension. Those changes affected both chaperone function and the ability to block fibril formation. A tail that looks like a minor appendage turns out to carry real weight. Understanding it could guide designs for protective proteins, and it sharpens the basic picture of how chaperones grip their targets.
plos-pone-0001146:
Young malaria mosquitoes die in large numbers, but the causes are poorly understood. Krijn Paaijmans and colleagues tested one everyday hazard, rainfall, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their subject was Anopheles gambiae, the main malaria mosquito of Africa, whose larvae live in small pools.

The team studied how rain affects larval mortality under conditions the insects actually face. Their title reports an unexpected result: losses of larvae due to rainfall were high. That matters for malaria control, because models of mosquito populations often overlook weather as a direct killer of the young stages.
plos-pone-0001246:
Genes can be cut and spliced in alternative ways, and one control point is a signal hidden inside an intron. Necat Havlioglu and colleagues characterized such a signal in the human caspase-2 gene, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Alternative splicing is an important level at which genes for programmed cell death are regulated.

The element, called In100, is a 100-nucleotide intronic sequence with upstream and downstream parts. The authors present it as an intronic signal for alternative splicing in the human genome. Since caspase-2 helps decide whether cells die, control of its splicing touches cancer and degeneration alike.
plos-pone-0001346:
Bartonella henselae is a bacterial pathogen spread from cats to people, causing cat scratch disease and other illnesses. Mardjan Arvand and colleagues typed isolates of the bacterium from three continents, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Previous investigations suggested that a limited subset of isolates may be associated with human disease.

Using multi-locus sequence typing, the authors reveal hypervirulent and feline-associated clones among the isolates. In plain terms, some family lines of the bacterium are much likelier to cause human disease than others. Such typing helps trace infections and understand what makes a clone dangerous.
plos-pone-0001446:
Qingjun Zhu and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gene that keeps cells young. The gene makes telomerase, an enzyme that can extend cell life. A protein called LSD1 trims chemical tags from DNA wrapping proteins. The team asked whether LSD1 helps switch the telomerase gene off as cells mature.

They show that LSD1 is needed to keep that gene hushed in normal cells. When LSD1 is lost, the gene wakes up. That wake up is a step many cancers take to grow without end. The finding names a guard whose loss may help tumors start, and a target worth study.
plos-pone-0001546:
Michael Cook and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on cheap barcode chips. Barcode arrays let labs track many cell strains at once via short DNA tags. Building such chips by the standard route is costly. The team built chips where tags bind without a fixed bond, at lower cost.

They checked the cheap chips with care, down to force scans of the surface. The chips read the tags as well as the costly kind. A cheaper chip opens pooled strain tests to more labs. It also scales to the huge libraries that gene screens now use.
plos-pone-0001646:
Kenichi Horisawa, Nobuhide Doi, and Hiroshi Yanagawa combined two lab tools to find protein partners faster, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In vitro display methods, such as mRNA display, can fish huge numbers of protein variants for ones that bind a target. The slow step came after: cloning and sequencing each hit, which let many true hits slip through as false negatives.

The authors instead read the selected pool with cDNA tiling arrays, chips that can detect many gene pieces at once. The full text explains the combined method, the test proteins they used, and how many more hits the array step recovered. A faster readout makes display screens more complete, which helps labs map how proteins interact inside cells.
plos-pone-0001746:
Struan F. A. Grant, Mingyao Li, Jonathan P. Bradfield, and their co-authors tested an obesity gene in children in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A genome-wide study of type 2 diabetes in adults had linked a variant in the FTO gene, rs9939609, to obesity. Whether the same gene region matters in childhood was the next question.

The team examined two stand-in variants for rs9939609 in children of Caucasian and African ancestry. They report finding a common tagging SNP associated with obesity in the children. The full text gives the child cohorts and the variant comparisons. Showing that an adult obesity locus acts already in childhood strengthens the case that FTO's effect is lifelong and starts early.
plos-pone-0001846:
Karin Anestål and co-authors studied how an antioxidant enzyme can be turned into a cell killer in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. SecTRAPs are selenium-compromised thioredoxin reductase-derived apoptotic proteins. They form from the selenoprotein thioredoxin reductase when its selenocysteine residue is targeted by electrophiles, or when the protein's tail is cut off.

Once converted, these proteins act as prooxidants that kill cells rather than protect them. The full text gives the conversion conditions and the cell death assays. A protective enzyme flipped into a killer is a possible cancer drug principle: tumor cells, rich in this enzyme, would arm the weapon themselves.
plos-pone-0001946:
Sebastien Guyader and Christina Burch tested a feeding theory on viruses that infect sea bacteria, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Optimal foraging theory predicts how a hunter should pick prey to gain the most food for its effort. In the sea, virus types that attack few host kinds tend to live where hosts are scarce, and broad attackers where hosts are many.

The pair adapted a classic diet model to these viruses, called bacteriophages. As the title states, the theory predicts the ecology of host range well, but not how that range evolved. A feeding rule can thus explain where viruses live, even if their history took another path.
plos-pone-0002046:
Jennifer Dan and co-authors tested a two-part vaccine trick against a fungal foe, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Dendritic cells are the immune system's scouts, and coating an antigen in mannose sugars targets it to their mannose receptors. Yet the response that follows is suboptimal, too weak to protect well.

The team used mannoproteins from the fungus Cryptococcus neoformans, a cause of lung and brain infection, plus CpG strands that trip a Toll-like alarm. As the title states, the two together stimulated dendritic cells cooperatively. A partner signal that lifts a weak vaccine response is a design worth reusing.
plos-pone-0002146:
Dinu Albeanu, Edward Soucy, Tomokazu Sato, and co-authors described a cheap light source for microscopes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fluorescence imaging, which makes tagged parts of cells glow, has grown fast thanks to new dyes and detectors. Standard widefield microscopes use arc lamps plus filters and shutters to control the light, and those parts cost money and wear out.

The team built arrays of LEDs, the small solid-state lights used in lamps and screens, to do the same job. Their setup offers a lower-cost and more efficient way to light samples. Cheaper imaging gear puts good microscopy within reach of more labs and classrooms.
plos-pone-0002246:
Douglas Axe, Brendan Dixon, and Philip Lu built a simplified world for testing ideas about protein evolution, described in PLOS ONE in 2008. Studying how proteins evolve is hard: the number of possible sequences is huge, folds are many. The links from sequence to shape to function are complex. Simple models may let researchers test broad claims that real proteins make hard to check.

Their system, called Stylus, models a protein and its proteome with functional rules that are not arbitrary. It lets users run evolution experiments in silico and see which claims hold. A clean test bed helps sort sound theory about protein evolution from mere storytelling.
plos-pone-0002346:
Jung Yoon Park, Mi-Ook Cho, Shanique Leonard, and co-authors examined the liver of mice that age too fast, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Unrepaired DNA damage is blamed as a cause of both cancer and aging. The Xpd TTD mice carry a mutation in the Xpd gene. It cripples DNA repair and transcription, giving them severe premature aging but, oddly, a reduced cancer rate.

The team looked at the balance between apoptosis, orderly cell death, and cell renewal in the liver. They found that balance tilted out of its normal homeostatic range. A liver that cannot match cell loss with cell replacement shows one concrete way DNA damage can age an organ.
plos-pone-0002446:
A research team led by Hensler reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Mary E. Hensler, Shigeki Miyamoto, Victor Nizet, and others. Its subject is group B Streptococcal β-Hemolysin/Cytolysin Directly Impairs Cardiomyocyte Viability and Function. Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis where myocardial dysfunction is an important contributor to poor outcome.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002546:
Work from Lindholm and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Eero Lindholm, Ekaterina Bakhtadze, Corrado Cilio, and others. Its subject is association between LTA , TNF and AGER Polymorphisms and Late Diabetic Complications. Several candidate genes on the short arm of chromosome 6 including the HLA locus, TNF.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002646:
Unknown led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was use of Evidence-Based practices in pregnancy and childbirth: s outh e ast a sia o ptimising r eproductive and c hild h ealth i n d eveloping countries project. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Unknown, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The burden of mortality and morbidity related to pregnancy and childbirth remains concentrated in developing countries. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002746:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Gilbert Q. Martinez and colleagues addresses a cytoplasmic domain mutation in ClC-Kb affects Long-Distance communication across the membrane. The catalog record names Gilbert Q. Martinez first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. ClC-Kb and ClC-Ka are homologous chloride channels that facilitate chloride homeostasis in the kidney and inner ear. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002846:
Roy A. Wise led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was cocaine serves as a peripheral interoceptive conditioned stimulus for central glutamate and dopamine release. Authorship is credited in the record to Roy A. Wise and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Intravenous injections of cocaine HCl are habit-forming because, among their many actions. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002946:
Helena Deus, Romesh Stanislaus, Diogo Veiga and co-authors proposed a semantic web model for biomedical data in 2008. Life science data are vast and varied, which defies easy linking between research groups. Rules for access and ownership add a further layer of difficulty to sharing.

Their model aims at integrative biomedical informatics, joining data while managing property and access permissions. Semantic web tools label data so machines can connect it across sources. Published in PLOS ONE, the paper is a design contribution: a management plan for data that must be both open to science and controlled.
plos-pone-0003046:
Lotfi Merabet, Roy Hamilton, Gottfried Schlaug and co-authors showed early visual cortex can be recruited for touch, fast and reversibly, in 2008. Loss of vision is tied to better touch and sound performance. Evidence suggests those gains link to the occipital visual cortex taking on non-visual processing.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team demonstrates rapid and reversible recruitment of early visual cortex for touch. The speed and reversibility are the news: the cortex can be borrowed without permanent rewiring. That informs rehabilitation training after vision loss and brain plasticity research generally. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003146:
Wendong Yu, Rajesh Ramakrishnan, Yan Wang and colleagues look for HIV helper genes in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. HIV-1 depends on the host cell's own factors to complete its copying cycle in CD4 T cells and macrophages, the two main cell types it infects. One key factor is Cyclin T1, part of a general system that extends RNA messages.

The authors examine genes that depend on Cyclin T1 in activated T cell and macrophage lines. They report those genes appear enriched for HIV-1 co-factors. Readers see a route to finding host proteins the virus needs. Such proteins can become targets for drugs that block the virus indirectly.
plos-pone-0003246:
Aki Ejima and Leslie C. Griffith test the role of sound in fruit fly courtship in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Finding a mating partner is a critical task for many organisms. It is in the interest of males to employ multiple sensory modalities to search for females. In Drosophila melanogaster, vision is thought to be the most important courtship stimulating cue at long distance, while chemical cues act up close.

The title reports that courtship initiation is stimulated by acoustic signals in this species. Readers learn that song matters from the very start, not only later in courtship. Fly song is a model for how nervous systems produce patterned behaviour.
plos-pone-0003346:
Mei Ding, Ryan S. King, Emily C. Berry and colleagues study embryo elongation in a worm in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The epidermal cells of the C. elegans embryo undergo coordinated cell shape changes that result in the morphogenetic process of elongation. The cytoskeletal ankyrin repeat protein VAB-19 is required for cell shape changes and localizes to cell-matrix attachment structures.

The title reports the cell signaling adaptor protein EPS-8 is essential for C. elegans epidermal elongation and interacts with the ankyrin repeat protein VAB-19. Readers follow two proteins working together at attachment points. Worm embryo shaping is a clear model for how tissues change form in development.
plos-pone-0007446:
Robin Craven and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was a toxin made by drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Community strains of this germ cause severe infections that destroy skin, soft tissue, and lung. Its alpha-hemolysin toxin is a key weapon in those infections. The team asked how the toxin stirs such strong inflammation.

They showed that alpha-hemolysin switches on the NLRP3 inflammasome, an alarm complex inside immune cells. The effect appeared in both human and mouse immune cells. Once triggered, the inflammasome drives the response that damages tissue. Explaining this trigger clarifies part of the germ's harmfulness. It also suggests that calming the inflammasome could limit the destruction these infections cause.
plos-pone-0007546:
Brenton Louie, Roger Higdon, and Eugene Kolker published a statistical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on predicting what proteins do. Thousands of proteins have unknown functions. Computers guess their jobs by comparing sequences to proteins already understood. One problem is that the guesses tend to be overly specific. The authors built a model relating sequence similarity to function similarity, to see where the overconfidence creeps in.

The model shows how much functional precision a given sequence match can honestly support. Beyond a point, close spelling does not justify close functional claims. Correcting that bias should make automated annotation more honest. Honest annotations matter because databases propagate guesses into thousands of later studies. The paper is a calibration tool for a workhorse method of modern biology. It tells predictors when to say less.
plos-pone-0007646:
Qiyao Wang and colleagues published a genome study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Edwardsiella tarda, a versatile fish pathogen. The bacterium causes edwardsiellosis, a devastating disease in aquaculture worldwide. It infects many fish species and can live inside host cells. The team sequenced the complete genome of strain EIB202, a highly virulent and multi-drug resistant isolate from China. With the full sequence in hand, they searched for the basis of its adaptability.

The genome reveals the toolkit behind the bacterium's broad host range and intracellular life. Genes for invading cells, surviving inside them, and resisting drugs all leave readable traces. Knowing the toolkit guides vaccine and treatment work in fish farming. It also helps track how such strains spread through the industry. A complete genome is a reference every later study will use. The pathogen's versatility is now written down to be studied.
plos-pone-0007746:
Vassiliki Kotoula and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tackles a practical problem in cancer diagnosis. Doctors test tumor tissue for mutations in a gene called KRAS. The result can predict whether a treatment will work.

Routine tumor samples are fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin, which damages DNA. The team assessed KRAS mutations on such real-world material. They used a sensitive real-time PCR method in a live diagnostic setting. Showing the test works on standard hospital samples is a key step. It brings mutation-guided treatment closer to everyday oncology practice.
plos-pone-0007846:
Alok Chakrabarti and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It characterizes the H5N1 flu viruses behind India's 2008 to 2009 outbreaks. Highly pathogenic bird flu hit poultry in West Bengal in early 2008. It then spread to three northeastern states, with dozens of outbreaks reported.

Sequencing the viruses revealed their family ties. The analysis points to a third separate introduction into India. It also raises the possibility that H5N1 had become endemic there. Knowing whether a virus is newly imported or locally rooted changes control strategy. The study sharpens that judgment for Indian authorities.
plos-pone-0007946:
Haijing Hu and Stephen Leppla measured how anthrax toxin enters immune cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Anthrax germs must beat the body's first defenses to start an infection, and their toxin dulls those defenses. The team used a lab-built marker protein to track entry cell by cell.

Watching the marker in fresh immune cells showed which cells take the toxin in and how fast. Cells that guard the body first are among those hit, which fits how the germ gains its early hold. A clear view of entry helps the search for drugs that block the toxin at the door.
plos-pone-0008046:
Andres Arenas and colleagues showed that lessons learned young stick with bees, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Honeybees learn which scents promise food, a skill their work depends on. The team trained bees at different ages and tested how long the lesson lasted.

Bees trained in early adulthood held the lesson far longer than bees trained later. Early experience thus shapes the older bee in a lasting way, much as it does in mammals. For bee keepers and farmers, the finding says the first days of a worker's life set the quality of the forager she becomes.
plos-pone-0008146:
Alexander Link and colleagues gave a common virus a role in colon cancer spread in PLOS ONE in 2009. JC virus infects most people quietly and harms few. Its DNA and its main protein, called T antigen, show up in about half of colorectal cancers, which raised a pointed question.

Cancer cells carrying the viral protein pushed into new tissue and migrated more strongly than those without it. A quiet passenger thus looks like an active accomplice in metastasis, the spread that makes this cancer deadly. The link may suggest new ways to flag or slow the worst cases.
plos-pone-0008246:
Guadalupe Andreani and colleagues studied two infections sharing the same cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Macrophages are a major target of HIV-1 and a reservoir where the virus persists. The same cells are targeted by Trypanosoma cruzi. That protozoan parasite causes Chagas disease, a major illness in the Americas. The team used human macrophages grown from monocytes for their tests.

They found the parasite inhibited HIV-1 replication in those cells. One infection thus interfered with the other inside shared host cells. The result may matter in regions where both diseases occur. It also reveals how pathogens interact within the immune system.
plos-pone-0008346:
Michael R. May and colleagues studied an ancient oak in southern California in PLOS ONE in 2009. Palmer's oak survives in scattered, isolated populations. These are presumably relicts of a wider range that shrank as the climate dried. That drying followed the end of the Pleistocene ice age. A recently discovered stand offered a test of that history.

The team investigated whether the stand is a single ancient clone. A clone persisting since the Pleistocene would be among the oldest living organisms. Genetic evidence can date and define such a stand. The study connects botany with deep climate history.
plos-pone-0008446:
Abigail Lamikanra and co-authors study severe malaria and blood loss in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Severe anemia is the most common grave form of malaria in areas where the disease is common. In long cases, the marrow makes red cell precursors in a flawed way. The body fails to replace red cells fast enough. The team look at hemozoin, a pigment left by the malaria parasite.

They find that hemozoin drives those precursor cells to die. That death helps explain why red cells are not replaced. The work names a direct cause of the anemia. It may point to ways to protect the marrow in malaria.
plos-pone-0008546:
Filippo Caschera and co-authors use robots to find new drug mixes in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their test case is a liposomal drug, a drug wrapped in tiny fat bubbles. Such a mix has many parts that act on each other. The parts can help or hinder each other in ways no one can predict. Trial and error by hand would be very slow. The team use a loop of fast tests guided by a computer model.

Each round of tests teaches the model which mixes work best. The model then picks the next round of mixes to try. The loop finds good mixes far faster than blind search. The same method could help tune other complex mixes.
plos-pone-0008646:
Matteo Bellone and co-authors study immune cells in mouse cancer in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Invariant NKT cells are a subset of T lymphocytes with innate effector functions. They aid establishment of adaptive T and B cell responses. iNKT cells play a spontaneous protective role against experimental tumors. The team ask if that protection needs tumor-specific cytotoxic T cells. They use mice that develop spontaneous carcinoma. CD1d presents lipid antigens to iNKT cells in this system.

They find iNKT cells control spontaneous carcinoma independently of cytotoxic T cells. Protection does not route through the classic killer cell arm. That independence suggests iNKT activation could help patients lacking strong cytotoxic responses. It broadens the rationale for iNKT-based cancer immunotherapy.
plos-pone-0008746:
Annie Frelet-Barrand, Sylvain Boutigny, Lucas Moyet, and colleagues offered a milk germ as a protein factory. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Membrane proteins are vital but hard to study. They shun water and occur in tiny natural amounts. Standard host cells often make them poorly or not at all. Plant membrane proteins were especially underserved by existing systems.

The food germ Lactococcus lactis took up Arabidopsis membrane protein genes. It produced both surface and internal membrane proteins in working form. A safe, food-grade host lowers the barrier to such work. Biochemists gain a friendlier route to hard proteins.
plos-pone-0008846:
Mónica López Fanarraga, Javier Bellido, Cristina Jaén, and colleagues tied one helper protein to three steps of cell division. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microtubules form the rails and spindle that organize dividing cells. Building them needs tubulin parts assembled by five cofactor proteins. One cofactor, TBCD, was known to help fold tubulin. Its wider duties in human cells were unclear.

TBCD proved to link centriole formation, spindle dynamics, and the final snip separating daughter cells. Losing it disrupted all three jobs. One helper thus coordinates the microtubule system end to end. The finding matters for cancers where division machinery runs wild.
plos-pone-0008946:
Jessica Dyszel and co-authors listed the genes that a bacterial signal-reader controls in E. coli, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The reader, SdiA, listens for chemical signals made by other kinds of bacteria. When those signals arrive, SdiA switches a set of genes on or off. One target strain was EHEC, an E. coli type that causes severe food poisoning.

The team compared gene activity with and without extra SdiA in the cell. Genes for movement, surface structures, and stress handling shifted under its control. The list shows how E. coli eavesdrops on its neighbours and adjusts. Understanding that chatter may suggest new ways to disarm harmful strains.
plos-pone-0009046:
Mariano Larzábal and co-authors designed molecular plugs for the needle E. coli uses to attack gut cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enteropathogenic E. coli causes severe diarrhoea, especially in children. It grips gut cells using a type three secretion system, a tiny injection needle. The needle also delivers proteins that let the germ hold on and cause disease.

The team built coiled-coil peptides shaped to jam that machinery. The peptides interfered with the secretion system in their tests. Blocking the needle disarms the germ without killing it outright. Such anti-virulence drugs might sidestep the resistance that antibiotics provoke.
plos-pone-0009146:
Ardina Grüber and co-authors solved pieces of a malaria protein that grabs red blood cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria parasites invade red blood cells to multiply. That invasion leans on many handshakes between parasite and cell proteins. Py235, from the mouse malaria Plasmodium yoelii, helps pick reticulocytes, the youngest red cells.

The team determined the structure of functional units in its binding domain. NBD94 is the part that grips nucleotides, the cell's energy packets. Structure at this detail exposes pockets a drug could block. Blocking the grip could keep the parasite out of blood cells.
plos-pone-0009246:
Eliyahu Khankin and co-authors published this kidney study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Erythropoietin is a hormone used to treat anemia in kidney patients. Many patients with end-stage renal disease respond poorly to it. Doctors then raise the dose again and again, often without reaching target blood counts.

The team investigated one suspect: a soluble form of the erythropoietin receptor floating in the blood. Such loose receptors could soak up the hormone before it reaches bone marrow. They report that this soluble receptor contributes to the resistance seen in these patients. The finding suggests a new way to predict, and perhaps reduce, poor responses.
plos-pone-0009346:
Michel Laurent, Jean Deschatrette, and Claire Wolfrom published this cell growth study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Populations of mammal cells often grow in long, slow waves. Their division rate rises and falls over long ranges, in dishes and in bodies alike. Such patterns mix random events with deterministic control.

The authors asked whether part of that control is chaotic, in the mathematical sense. Chaos means orderly rules producing hard-to-predict swings. They unmasked chaotic attributes hidden in time series from living cell populations. Finding chaos in growth data would change how biologists model cell populations, since chaotic systems defy long-range forecasts even when fully lawful.
plos-pone-0011446:
Kaori Tsurui, Atsushi Honma, and Takayoshi Nishida tested camouflage in a small grasshopper in 2010. Tetrix japonica comes in several color patterns within one species, and each pattern is a bet on blending into a particular ground surface. The team placed the different forms against different microhabitat backgrounds and measured how well each hid.

Some patterns hid superbly on one background and poorly on another, so no single form won everywhere. That patchwork result explains how several patterns can persist in one population: each microhabitat favors its own best disguise. The experiments are a neat field test of natural selection's oldest trick. For ecology, the study shows why variation itself can be the adaptation, when the world an animal must match is a mosaic rather than one flat color.
plos-pone-0011546:
Fei Chen and co-authors built a gene catalog in 2010 for America's two great farmed catfish. Channel catfish and blue catfish anchor a large aquaculture industry, and their hybrids are prized, yet their genetic toolkits lagged far behind those of other farmed animals. The team identified and characterized full-length cDNAs, complete copies of active genes, from both species.

Full-length copies matter because partial fragments leave a gene's true start, end, and protein uncertain. With complete sequences, breeders can track traits, design accurate tests, and compare the two species gene by gene. The catalog equips biologists to improve growth, disease resistance, and feed efficiency in fish that supply a large share of farmed freshwater protein. It also enables the hybrid's genetics to be managed deliberately rather than by habit.
plos-pone-0011646:
Anna Metaxas and Noreen Kelly compared how deep-sea communities renew themselves, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vent and seep habitats run on chemicals rather than sunlight and occur as small, scattered patches on the dark seafloor. Their animal communities include many species found nowhere else, and they must recover from disturbance using drifting larvae.

The authors asked whether larval supply and settlement differ among these chemosynthetic settings. Their comparison shows how uneven the connection between patches can be. That unevenness matters for protecting deep-sea sites, because a damaged community can only recover if larvae arrive from elsewhere.
plos-pone-0011746:
Dashdemberel Narantuya and co-authors transplanted human immune cells into stroke-damaged rat brains, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microglia are the brain's resident immune and clean-up cells, releasing signals and growth factors after injury that shape how damage unfolds. Their net effect after stroke can help or harm, depending on context.

The team grafted human microglia into rats with focal ischaemia, a local loss of blood flow. The transplanted cells induced protection of brain tissue and improved behaviour. A cross-species rescue like this suggests donor microglia could one day aid stroke recovery.
plos-pone-0011846:
Stephen Hughes and colleagues ran a small pilot study in 2010 on what a surgical tourniquet does to the body beyond stopping blood flow. Tourniquets are routine in upper limb bone surgery, keeping the field clear while surgeons work. Ten patients having planned operations agreed to give blood samples from the arm at set points.

Comparing those samples showed that surgery with a tourniquet raised signs of inflammation and shifted markers tied to white blood cells, clotting, and the lining of blood vessels. The changes suggest the squeeze and release leaves a wider imprint on the blood than surgeons usually track. Knowing that imprint matters when weighing how long a tourniquet should stay on.
plos-pone-0011946:
Taryn Roberts, Paul McGreevy, and Michael Valenzuela reported in 2010 that life with humans has turned and reshaped the brain of the pet dog. Dog breeds vary a great deal in skull shape, from long-nosed to flat-faced. What no one had checked was whether the brain inside is laid out in new ways to match.

By looking at the brain's midline shape across breeds, the team found signs that the brain has been rotated and its parts re-laid as the skull changed. Breeding for short faces and other traits has thus quietly re-posed the brain itself. That fact may help explain why breeds act so unlike each other, and it adds a hidden cost to breeding for looks alone.
plos-pone-0012046:
Jeffrey Chow, Eili Klein, and Ramanan Laxminarayan weighed in 2010 whether a biofortified mustard could fight vitamin A deficiency in India at a fair cost. Deficiency there raises the risk of severe illness and death, especially in children. The standing World Health Organization remedy is periodic high-dose supplements, which work but must be delivered again and again.

Golden Mustard, bred to carry extra vitamin A precursor in a food people already eat, offers a different delivery route. A cost-effectiveness analysis compares that route against supplements on equal terms. For policy, the useful question is not whether the crop works in principle but whether each case prevented costs less than the alternatives.
plos-pone-0012146:
Clelia Gasparini, Leigh Simmons, and Maxine Beveridge studied sperm competition in a small tropical fish for PLOS ONE in 2010. When several males mate with one female, their sperm race to fertilize her eggs, and traits that win that race should spread. Numbers clearly matter, since more sperm means more tickets in the draw, but whether swimming quality matters was far less sure.

In the green swordtail, faster-swimming sperm predicted which males won fertilizations. That ties a simple lab measurement, swimming speed, to real reproductive success. It helps explain how male traits evolve under this hidden contest, and it may guide breeding work in fish farms and conservation programs.
plos-pone-0012246:
Maria Vittoria Barone, Merlin Nanayakkara, Giovanni Paolella, and co-authors tracked a wheat peptide inside gut cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Celiac disease, an immune reaction to wheat gluten affecting about one person in a hundred, begins in a particular genetic setting, yet the trigger steps are still being pieced together. One gluten fragment is known to disturb gut cells directly, apart from the immune attack.

They found the fragment settles into the cell's recycling vesicles and jams their maturation. A jam in that housekeeping traffic could help explain how the fragment stresses the gut lining before immunity joins in. Each early step clarified is a possible point for a drug to protect people who cannot fully avoid gluten.
plos-pone-0012346:
John Reganold, Preston Andrews, Jennifer Reeve and fellow researchers compared organic and standard strawberry farms in a 2010 PLOS ONE study from California fields. Shoppers often pay more for organic fruit because they expect better taste, more nutrition, and healthier soil. The team set out to test those beliefs side by side on real working farms.

They measured fruit quality, taste, nutrition, and soil health across matched farm pairs. Organic berries and soils scored higher on many of the tests, though not on every single one. Because the study used commercial farms rather than lab plots, its results speak directly to shoppers, growers, and anyone weighing the true value of organic food.
plos-pone-0012446:
Nuno Araújo, José Andrade and Hans Herrmann modeled tactical voting in simple winner-take-all elections, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The authors ask how often elections end in landslides and how often in close races. Ballot results from several large countries showed odd but universal patterns that simple models had not matched.

Adding tactical voters — people who back a viable candidate rather than a hopeless favorite — made the model reproduce those patterns. Strategic behavior, in other words, shapes election statistics at national scale. The work gives election watchers a baseline for spotting results that look truly abnormal rather than merely surprising.
plos-pone-0012546:
Dawn Loh, Juliana Navarro, Arkady Hagopian and colleagues scrambled the light cycle of mice and tested their memory, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Body clocks govern learning and memory circuits, including the amygdala, which stores fear associations. Frequent flyers and shift workers know the fog of jet lag, but its direct effect on stored memories was untested in a controlled model.

Rapid shifts of the light-dark cycle disrupted the mice's memory of conditioned fear. The memories did not merely form poorly; recall itself suffered after schedule chaos. The work gives biological weight to complaints from night-shift workers and suggests sleep timing belongs in memory research.
plos-pone-0012646:
Downes, Pekalski, Angus and co-authors reported that a weaker version of an immune gene can guard against type 1 diabetes. The gene, IFIH1, helps cells sense viral RNA and launch a defence. Earlier work had already tied it to diabetes, in which the immune system attacks the pancreas.

Their 2010 study shows that having less of this gene's activity lowers diabetes risk. That flips the usual story of a gene defect causing harm, since here reduced action protects. It hints that calming this virus sensor might one day help prevent the disease.
plos-pone-0012746:
Jogi, Rono, Lund and co-authors slowed skin healing in mice by blocking one clot-dissolving activator. Wound repair needs plasmin and related enzymes to clear paths for new skin. Mice lacking plasminogen already heal very slowly, setting the baseline for their 2010 study.

They used an antibody to neutralise uPA in mice that also lacked tPA, the other main activator. Healing slowed further and plasmin formation dropped, proving uPA's own share in repair. Knowing each activator's share helps design wound treatments that speed safe healing.  Their antibody tool let them switch one activator off at will.
pmc-2206446:
Mehta, Kellum, Shah, and co-authors report the work of the Acute Kidney Injury Network. Acute kidney injury is a complex, sudden loss of kidney function. At the time, the field had no accepted shared definition of the condition, which held back care and research.

The network sought a uniform standard for diagnosing and grading kidney injury. Common terms would let doctors manage patients more consistently and let researchers compare studies across hospitals. The report lays out an initiative for joint clinical and lab research aimed at improving outcomes for a common and dangerous problem.
pmc-3760646:
Witwer, Buzas, Bemis, and co-authors argue for standardisation in extracellular vesicle research. Publications on extracellular RNA and vesicles had highlighted their potential as disease biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Those findings created a paradigm shift, most prominently in cancer and diagnostics.

Yet labs collected, isolated, and analysed samples in very different ways, so results clashed. The authors propose shared standards for each step. Common methods would let the young field compare results honestly and speed the move of vesicle tests into clinics.  Funding for shared standards work followed, reflecting how seriously the field took it.
pmc-3995046:
Lopez-Calderon and Luck presented ERPLAB in 2014, a free toolbox for brain signal research. It works with event-related potentials, small voltage changes in the scalp signal that follow a sight, sound, or task. ERPLAB runs inside MATLAB and is built to work closely with EEGLAB, a widely used open toolbox.

ERPLAB handles the later steps of work, such as sorting trials, averaging signals, and measuring peaks and timing. Its screens let users run these steps without writing much code. Brain labs use it to study attention, memory, and language, with a shared tool that makes results easier to check and repeat.
pmc-4310146:
Methley, Campbell, Chew-Graham, and their co-authors compared search tools for qualitative reviews in 2014. Systematic reviews of qualitative research were growing in health care. Many teams reported trouble searching the literature with PICO, a tool built for clinical questions.

A newer tool, SPIDER, was designed for qualitative and mixed methods studies. The study compared PICO, its variant PICOS, and SPIDER for sensitivity and specificity in real searches. Knowing which tool finds the right papers without floods of junk saves reviewers weeks of work. The findings guide teams planning reviews of patient experience and other qualitative topics.
pmc-6259146:
Jin Dai and Russell Mumper reviewed plant phenolics in 2010. Phenolics are the most common secondary compounds made by plants. They drew attention for strong antioxidant action and possible roles in preventing disease.

The review covers how phenolics are extracted from plant material and measured in the lab. It then surveys evidence that they can slow oxidation and, in cell and animal studies, hinder cancer growth. Human proof was thinner at the time, and dose and absorption remain hard problems. Food and supplement researchers still use it as a broad survey of the field.
pmc-6323946:
Adam Frankish, Mark Diekhans, Anne-Maud Ferreira, and coauthors described GENCODE annotation for human and mouse in 2018. Accurate gene maps are a basic need for genome biology and clinical work. For over fifteen years the GENCODE group has produced reference annotation.

Their process blends computer prediction with human review to place genes and transcripts. Each release refines boundaries and adds newly found transcripts, including long non-coding RNAs. Most human genome studies align their results to GENCODE coordinates. The paper explains methods and quality checks so users know what the map rests on.
plos-pone-0359646:
Jolinda Pollock and co-authors characterized in 2026 a strain of Escherichia coli bacteria taken from dairy bred calves that had fallen ill. The strain belongs to the O78 group and resembles types known for causing disease in poultry. The calves showed an atypical form of colisepticaemia, a blood infection by E. coli that usually follows a more familiar pattern.

The team describes the strain's traits in detail, including the fact that it resists multiple antibiotics. A poultry-like strain turning up in calves raises questions about how such bacteria move between animal species and through farm environments. Multidrug resistance in farm animals also matters beyond the farm, since resistance can travel through food chains and waste into wider circulation.
plos-pone-0358546:
Margaret Wingerd and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about a gut parasite in pet cats. Giardia duodenalis infects domestic cats across the United States and Canada. The authors measure its prevalence and judge its zoonotic potential, the chance of it passing to people.

A parasite shared between cats and humans matters for households, especially where children or people with weak immunity live with pets. Prevalence figures tell veterinarians how often to expect this infection and test for it. Public health readers also gain from knowing how much of the human risk from Giardia plausibly comes through cats.
plos-pone-0359346:
Maxime Colomb and Julien Perret published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It describes systematic modelling of building land use at large scale, enriched with historical detail. The work fuses massive and heterogeneous datasets, records from many sources that were never designed to fit together.

Land use histories tell planners how neighborhoods grew and which uses persisted or vanished. Building that record by hand for a whole city is impossible, so an automated, systematic model is the only route. Urban historians and planning offices are the readers who gain a past-aware map of building use from this fusion work.
plos-pone-0359946:
Gideon Nwankwo and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on maternal healthcare in Nigeria. It studies what decides whether women keep using maternal care steadily, from pregnancy through delivery and beyond. The evidence comes from Nigeria's 2024 Demographic and Health Survey.

Many women start antenatal care but drop out before skilled delivery, breaking the continuum where risk peaks. National survey evidence shows which social and economic factors hold women in care or push them out. Nigerian health planners designing maternal programs are the readers who can act on those determinants.
plos-pone-0359846: Sangsiwarit and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE lab study on blood disease and infection risk. They took neutrophils, a front-line white blood cell, from people with beta-thalassemia. Outside the body, they exposed those cells to Pythium insidiosum, a water mold that can cause severe illness. They then checked how the cells' working behavior changed. The results bear on why these patients may fight this infection poorly.
plos-pone-0358746: Monfort Sanchez and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a low-cost way to check cell barriers. Labs often grow cells in a flat sheet to mimic the linings of the gut or lungs. The team tested cheap, clinic-approved glowing dyes as a way to judge whether those sheets stay sealed. A cheap, safe check could widen barrier testing in labs with small budgets.

Jingcong Li and three colleagues improve the neural networks that solve physics equations by teaching them where to concentrate, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Physics informed networks learn a solution while respecting the governing equation at sampled points, but they spread effort evenly and under learn the hard regions. Their system closes a feedback loop. The equation's own error at each point estimates how difficult that point is. That estimate stretches the physical constraint around hard points. It also shifts training weight toward them.

Tested across five network designs on three one dimensional problems, the method took the lowest error on every benchmark. It cut the runner up method's aggregate error by roughly a fifth to three fifths, depending on the problem. Higher dimensional and fluid test cases followed. The principle is portable: a solver that notices its own confusion can spend its budget where confusion lives.
plos-pone-0341946:
Ahmet Süerdem, Svetlomir Zdravkov, and Martin J Ivanov model how knowledge, conspiracy thinking, and mistrust of science connect across Europe, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Two camps dominate debate: one says more knowledge cures mistrust, the other says worldviews coexist. Using cross national survey data gathered during the COVID-19 pandemic, the team fitted a multilevel model. It lets the pathway run at personal and regional levels simultaneously. They tested what strengthens or weakens it.

Conspiratorial reasoning turned out to be the bridge. It significantly carried the effect of scientific knowledge toward mistrust at both levels of the model. The strength of the pathway shifted with information engagement, regional value climates, and religiosity. Knowledge, the authors conclude, is a conditional resource: in some minds and regions it buffers mistrust, in others it barely dents it. Science communication that ignores the conspiratorial step will misread its audience.
plos-pone-0352346:
Jay Kirkham led a team of seven authors studying how North Atlantic right whales feed, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These whales are critically endangered, so knowing how they find and take food helps protect them. The team combined motion tags on free-swimming whales with camera checks and machine learning.

Kirkham's method lets researchers read feeding events straight from tag data, without watching each whale. That means feeding can be tracked at scale, in places and seasons observers rarely reach. Knowing where and how right whales feed guides shipping and fishing rules meant to keep them alive. With so few whales left, each gain in understanding carries unusual weight.
plos-pone-0358046:
Cleofé Peña-Gómez, Bernat Sunyer-Grau, and Marc Argilés studied how light color affects the brain, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Light does more than let us see; different wavelengths reach brain systems that control eye movement and attention. The team measured how exposure to different wavelengths changes activity in those cortical areas.

Peña-Gómez and her colleagues found wavelength-specific effects on the systems that aim the eyes and focus attention. That matters for lighting design in schools and offices, and for screen habits that fill evenings with blue-rich light. It also informs therapies that use light to shift alertness. The study adds brain-level evidence to a field often guided by comfort alone.
plos-pone-0358246:
Alejandro Leyva and M Khalid Khan Niazi subtyped pancreatic cancer patient by patient, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Pancreatic cancer needs finer subtypes if treatment is to be matched to each tumor. The pair integrated three data layers for each patient: RNA expression, methylation-based clues to replication timing, and the tumor's appearance under the microscope.

Leyva's multi-layer integration sorts tumors more precisely than any single data type could. Patient-specific subtyping matters because two tumors with the same name can behave very differently. Better sorting can guide trials, pairing each subtype with drugs aimed at its biology. Pancreatic cancer's poor outcomes make every gain in precision count, and integration methods like this are a plausible route.
plos-pone-0357346:
Titilayo T Tajudeen led a team of four authors mapping retreating coastal forests, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Coastal forests are shrinking under pressure from storms, sea level rise, and land clearing. Satellites can track that retreat, but reading their images by hand is slow. The team applied convolutional neural networks to different kinds of satellite imagery.

Tajudeen's AI-generated maps give conservationists the retreat's true extent, free from guesswork. Comparing imagery types shows which source gives the most reliable map for the least cost. Coastal forests protect shorelines and store carbon, so their loss is a double blow. Timely maps let agencies target planting and protection where retreat is fastest, and prove losses that ground surveys would miss.
plos-pone-0357146:
Senad Kolar and coauthors published a 2026 pilot study in PLOS ONE on whether autism evaluations by video still work when the connection is bad. Telehealth widens access to diagnosis, but a freezing screen could hide the fleeting behaviors assessors must catch. Using a fiber-optic test setup, the team created four freeze patterns by throttling the signal, then had blinded psychologists score children's videos under each degraded condition.

Scoring eroded gradually rather than collapsing. Past clear technical thresholds, freezes grew frequent. The items most at risk were the time-sensitive ones. Spontaneous joint attention, blending gaze with behavior, and echoed or unusual language were several times more likely to be marked unscorable. Yet overall scores stayed stable, no single item failed significance after correction, and raters agreed strongly under mild conditions. Video assessment is supported as a first-line option while connections stay above the identified thresholds, preferring wired links.
plos-pone-0356746:
Valia Pernidaki and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on fathers' mental health when a preterm birth threatens or happens. Mothers' distress in that situation is well documented; fathers are an afterthought. Just over one hundred men completed depression and anxiety scales during pregnancy and six weeks after the birth. They were sorted into a term-birth group and two risk groups: threatened preterm birth ending at term, and threatened ending early.

During pregnancy, fathers whose babies did arrive early carried clearly higher depression and anxiety than controls, while the threatened-but-term group showed weak signs of depression. Both risk groups had more men crossing the elevated-depression threshold than controls did. After birth, depression gaps closed, but anxiety stayed higher in the actual preterm group, and the threatened-but-term fathers sat in between. A threatened preterm birth alone, they conclude, marks a father for support.
plos-pone-0357446:

Published in 2026, the work uses satellite images to map land cover across the whole country rather than a few reserves. That wider view matters because past estimates for Ghana varied a lot and left policy makers unsure of the scale of loss.

Ghana lost a large stretch of forest over the decade, and yearly loss sped up in the second half of the period. Farm growth caused most of the clearing, while mining caused a smaller share but grew fastest of all land uses. plos-pone-0356646:

plos-pone-0357046:
Qian Wen and co-authors design fast-settling equation systems for solving a broad class of balance problems in math, called mixed equilibrium problems. Such problems model fair points where competing effects cancel, from traffic to markets. Their systems are built to reach solutions fast. One reaches the answer within a finite time. The other reaches it within a time the user fixes in advance. Both hold no matter where the system starts, under stated conditions on the problem's shape.

The authors prove existence and uniqueness of the answer, show the underlying system is stable, and turn it into a step-by-step algorithm with steady convergence. Computer tests found the preset-time version fastest of the variants. An application to recovering sparse signals showed the method working outside pure theory. The paper is fully mathematical, aimed at optimization specialists.
plos-pone-0355946:
Saadi M Saleh and a multinational team survey more than six thousand doctors across twelve Middle East and North African countries about chest pain. Doctors carry heavy stress and heart risk themselves, yet no large regional study had measured their own symptoms. A standard angina questionnaire sorted pain into definite and possible categories, and validated scales screened for anxiety and panic alongside work and health habits.

About one in eight doctors met the bar for definite angina-type pain, and nearly half reported possible angina-type pain, strikingly high for a working population. Panic disorder was the single strongest predictor, ahead of physical illness, lost sleep, anxiety, obesity, and female sex, and every kind of nicotine use added risk. plos-pone-0356146:
Qin Yu and Tao Mai build a translation system aimed at the hardest words in English news. The targets are culturally loaded terms, metaphors, and institutional names. Such items lack support in training data. Such long-tail items drift in meaning or lose their cultural charge in standard machine translation. Their design first squeezes text into a sparse code. The code spotlights cultural elements. Then it rebuilds the translation step by step. A diffusion process does the rebuilding, guided by gates and a cultural knowledge base.

On long news sentences, the system beat three mainstream rivals on two standard quality scores. On unseen vocabulary, it kept accuracy and recall well above the baselines. So the authors report. Yu and Mai present the hybrid as a route to translations that carry culture, not just words.
plos-pone-0355846:
Debrup Ghosh and colleagues collected soils from twenty sites across the Indo-Gangetic Plain in India and watched how iron escapes from them over time under different moisture levels. Iron matters because crops there often go short of it even in iron-rich ground, since it locks into minerals that roots cannot use. Their 2026 incubation study paired release measurements with chemical models of iron's forms.

Wetter soil and longer incubation both changed how much iron came free. Acidic conditions and salt content held iron back, while clay-rich soil that holds more water released more. The findings help explain why iron fertilizer often disappoints in these soils and suggest moisture management as part of the fix for iron-hungry crops.
plos-pone-0356546:
Dominic Dankwah Agyei and colleagues surveyed 237 researchers in Ghana about diamond open access, the publishing model where neither readers nor authors pay. Their 2026 cross-sectional study asked what researchers know about the model, where they learned it, and how they judge its benefits, then looked for patterns by age, rank, institution, and qualifications.

Awareness was thin. Two thirds had never heard of diamond open access, over half had never published open access at all, and few could identify the standard open license. Most who knew the model heard of it from colleagues, not institutions. Knowledge rose with seniority and qualifications. The authors call on Ghanaian universities to teach open publishing properly and fund it, rather than leaving equity in publishing to chance.
plos-pone-0318046:
Nunik Maharani and colleagues turned oil palm plantation workers into wildlife scientists. They piloted a monitoring system across seven Indonesian estates over five years. Their 2026 report describes how 3,950 employees logged wildlife sightings through a structured scheme. Management support and rewards backed the scheme. The team shows how the resulting flood of records can estimate where species actually live.

The haul was large: nearly 150,000 observations. They covered almost seven hundred animal species and close to two hundred plants. The cost per hectare ran far below conventional surveys. plos-pone-0356246:
Ahmad Adawy and seven colleagues trace how a marker on white blood cells changes after liver surgery in mice, in this 2026 study. Neutrophils, the first-responder immune cells, can either injure the liver or help it regrow after part is removed. The team combined gene-activity data with direct cell measurement in mouse livers after seventy percent of the organ was removed. They focused on a surface protein called Cd14, which earlier screens had flagged in activated liver neutrophils.

Both the gene and the protein surged in liver neutrophils, peaking a day after surgery. The protein was linked to two signaling pathways known to drive liver cell division, which led the authors to identify it as a badge of a pro-regeneration neutrophil type. They propose Cd14 as a possible therapeutic target for boosting liver regrowth after surgery, while noting the finding comes from mouse work.

White button mushrooms grow on a casing layer, which growers usually discard after use. Their 2026 study tested seven casing mixes and five feed supplements in a field experiment, then optimised the results mathematically.

The winning mix reused two-fifths recycled soil alongside peat, sugarcane residue, and minerals. Corn grit as a supplement beat the other feeds, lifting both yield and profit. The chosen pairing scored well across all three goals at once. Eslamizadeh and colleagues present the result as a circular-economy option for growers who must weigh money, food value, and waste together.
plos-pone-0355546:
Rebecca Gordon and co-authors use an adoption study to separate how parental stress reaches children through birth ties, womb environment, and daily rearing. Stress in parents can echo in children's self-control, but the pathway matters for any remedy. Their 2026 study follows families in a long-running adoption cohort where children were placed near birth.

The design links birth mothers' life stress to teenagers' effortful control through the children's daily cortisol rhythm, a stress-hormone pattern. It then asks whether adoptive mothers' or fathers' own stressful events strengthen or soften that chain. Because birth and rearing parents differ, genetic and prenatal routes can be told apart from household ones. The authors frame the work as a map for targeted family support.
plos-pone-0345346:
Daniel Snape and co-authors tested whether five days of heat training protects athletes' kidneys as well as their circulation. Heat acclimation is known to steady heart and temperature control, but kidney stress during hot exercise was a worry. Their 2026 trial randomised fourteen trained men to hot training or mild-condition exercise, with heat tests before and after.

Heat training lowered resting heart rate, expanded blood plasma volume, and raised sweat losses, the classic adaptation pattern. A fluid-balance hormone that spiked during the first heat test no longer rose after training. One kidney stress marker rose only in the control group during the first test, and another stayed flat throughout. Snape and colleagues conclude short acclimation helps without obvious kidney cost.
plos-pone-0355646:
Yaxiang Gong, Jiafu Wen, and Wenqi Liu test in 2026 a new way to make a plant compound called puerarin dissolve better in water. Poor dissolving limits how well the compound can be taken by mouth. Their method melts the material while blasting it with sound, then checks the result with light tests and several tools that probe crystal shape and heat behaviour.

Treated puerarin dissolved more and faster, with smaller grains that tended to clump. Its crystal form changed to a water holding form, and part of it lost ordered structure altogether. The authors link the gain to those two changes and suggest the method could improve oral products.
plos-pone-0339746:
Amanda Santos and colleagues develop in 2026 a new lab stain to diagnose a skin disease caused by Leishmania parasites in Brazil. They built an antibody that targets a parasite protein, first checking it on infected hamster tissue and parasite extracts. Then they tested the stain on skin samples from about a hundred patients with suspected disease, against a DNA test as the standard.

The new stain found a bit over half of true cases, slightly more than direct viewing or standard tissue checks, and it was almost always right when it said negative. Combining methods raised accuracy further. The authors say wider testing could earn it a routine place.
plos-pone-0355046:
