More than six hundred patients at two large hospitals described which herbal products they took and whether they told their doctors. The team then checked flagged herb and drug combinations against several interaction databases.

Many patients never disclosed their herbal use, and the databases often disagreed about the same combinations, leaving regional plants poorly covered. Phan calls for routine questions about herbs during care, better clinician training, and safety tools that include local botanical knowledge.
plos-pone-0354246:
Wei Zhang and Liangli Chen published this 2026 mathematics paper on solving two-dimensional equations that mix integrals and derivatives, a class arising in physics and engineering. Their method builds solutions from barycentric rational interpolation, a scheme prized for being steady and exact, paired with a precise counting rule.

They derived the full solution procedure, proved error bounds and that it settles, and tested the method on worked examples. Results matched the theory, confirming it was highly exact for both straight-line and nonlinear versions of these equations. Zhang and Chen aim the method at problems where older solvers lose precision.
plos-pone-0354146:
Kerle-Malcharek and colleagues, in a 2026 study, show how animal tracking tags can save battery by thinking before they transmit. Tags that ride on wild animals collect rich movement data, and newer tags send it by WiFi, which drains power fast. Sending everything shortens the tag's working life.

Their fix puts a tiny decision tree, a simple machine learning model, on the tag itself. The tree reads sensor data and recognizes a chosen behavior, such as feeding or resting. The tag then sends only data tied to moments that matter and holds back the rest. On a current commercial tag, this filtering cut energy use for transmission by a clear margin in realistic tests. Gyroscope data, usually processed later on a computer, proved especially useful on the tag. The team shares a full pipeline, from training data to tag-ready software, so other animal researchers can copy the trick.
plos-pone-0354346:
Adelle Holder, Henry DeBruin, and Jesse Sestito tackle a bottleneck in computer-aided design in this 2026 PLOS ONE methods paper. Bayesian optimisation searches for good designs by testing one candidate at a time, which wastes time when many tests could run in parallel. Existing parallel versions are usually built from scratch, ignoring a large library of proven one-at-a-time methods.

Their fix wraps any compatible sequential method in a penalty scheme that steers each batch of tests apart, so the batch covers fresh ground instead of repeating itself. Two converted methods matched established parallel tools on solution quality and beat them on real time. Designers gain a shortcut: upgrade familiar methods rather than rebuild them.
plos-pone-0353946:
Isabel Cervantes-Camacho and five colleagues reconstruct the life history of lane snapper in the Gulf waters off southern Mexico, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The fish supports busy commercial and recreational catches off Yucatan, yet basic facts like lifespan and natural death rates were missing. From more than a thousand landed fish, the team aged several hundred by counting yearly rings in their ear stones.

Ages ran from youngsters under a year to sixteen years in females. Comparing several growth curves with Bayesian methods, the classic von Bertalanffy model fit both sexes best. Solid age and growth numbers let managers set catch rules that a fishery can sustain instead of guessing.
plos-pone-0352146:
Jia Wang and Xiaoyang Dong publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for a trial of ear-based nerve stimulation to help stroke survivors move again. Stimulating the vagus nerve through the skin of both ears may beat the usual one-ear approach, judging by earlier small studies. Their planned multicentre trial will enrol one hundred and fourteen patients whose stroke left one side of the body weak.

Patients will be assigned at random to stimulation of both ears, one ear, or a control treatment, with patients and assessors kept unaware of who got what. The trial aims for the full limb picture, not just the arm. Results should show whether the bilateral method deserves a place in stroke rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0353846:
Chunhui Luo and six colleagues treat grey cast iron with laser-driven cavitation and test whether the treated surface resists corrosion better, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The process fires laser pulses into liquid so collapsing bubbles hammer the metal surface, hardening it without contact. The team varied laser energy and focus, and tried the treatment with and without a thin aluminium shield layer laid over the iron.

The shield clearly helped, shielding the surface from laser burn and bubble erosion, and corrosion resistance improved as laser energy rose — up to a point, after which it fell away again. Focus distance mattered less. For foundries, the recipe suggests a cheap surface upgrade for iron parts that must survive wet, corrosive work.
plos-pone-0353746:
Omar Saadani and six colleagues pair faba beans with helpful root bacteria. Their goal is to clean soil poisoned by lead and cadmium. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The beans grew in soil spiked at three levels. Some plants got a three-strain bacterial mix. The mix promotes plant growth and tolerates metals. The bacteria colonise the roots. They help the plant thrive in hostile ground.

The partnership worked best in the middle soil. Shoots grew heavier there. Root nodules flourished. The shoots pulled up far more lead and cadmium than plain plants. Cadmium uptake rose several times over. Protective chemistry in the roots rose too. In heavier soil the gains faded. That marks the practical limit of this gentle cleanup method.
plos-pone-0350946:
Jelto Branding and four colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study on microphones for listening to insects, a tool hoped to help with pest control and wildlife surveying. Systems that recognize insects by sound work in the lab but struggle outdoors, and the authors suspected cheap microphones are part of the problem. They compared a high-end, low-noise measurement array against an inexpensive array of the kind built into home voice assistants.

Experiments and simulations showed the sensitive array could record and identify far smaller, quieter insects. The cheap array still recognized some species, even with background noise added. The authors conclude that progress in acoustic insect monitoring needs microphones built for the job, since general-purpose hardware quietly caps what the software can achieve.
plos-pone-0330146:
Time Fukuda and five co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study building a survey scale that measures how anxious Japanese adults feel about COVID-19 vaccination. Such anxiety is a feeling, distinct from general vaccine doubt. No tested Japanese tool captured it. Five hundred adults filled in the new twenty-five-item scale twice, four weeks apart. They also answered measures of fear, readiness to vaccinate, and belief in conspiracies.

The scale settled into three parts. One part covers anxiety tied to trust in vaccines. One covers emotional symptoms. One covers worry about catching the virus even after a shot. Scores stayed steady over time. They also lined up well with the other measures, rising with fear and conspiracy belief, and falling as readiness rose. The authors argue that health messages should speak to feelings, not just give risk facts.
plos-pone-0352446:
Anna-Chiara Barta and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One DNA barcoding study updating Austria's inventory of woodlice, the land-dwelling crustaceans that recycle dead plant matter in soils. Austria's species list had not been reviewed in nearly fifty years. The team generated more than five hundred genetic barcodes from fresh specimens and even managed to sequence DNA from historic museum specimens.

The barcodes covered about three-quarters of the known Austrian species and added two species never before recorded in the country. Genetic splits inside several named species were deep enough to suggest hidden, unrecognized species, and in one case the team found matching subtle body differences to back the split. Older museum material worked best with a repaired short-barcode method. The dataset now anchors Austria's national barcode library for soil wildlife monitoring.
plos-pone-0350846:
Simone Luongo and three colleagues explore why luxury fashion houses are opening hotels and restaurants. Their 2026 study is qualitative, built on interviews with industry stakeholders. Fashion brands from catwalk names now serve meals and rent rooms. The authors ask what drives that leap, and where sustainability fits in.

Interviewees said the ventures deepen the brand experience beyond clothing. A stay or dinner lets customers live inside the brand's world. That strengthens engagement and loyalty. Sustainability showed up in both backstage operations and customer-facing touches. Its depth varied widely between companies, though. Aligning a fashion identity with hospitality service proved genuinely hard. The study gives managers a map of the rewards and the friction in crossing industries.
plos-pone-0352246:
David Sjöström and seven colleagues set out a trial protocol, published in 2026, for psilocybin therapy in anorexia nervosa. Anorexia is a severe eating disorder that often begins in adolescence. It carries high death and relapse rates. Standard psychological and nutritional care helps many patients, yet outcomes stay disappointing. Psilocybin has shown early promise in other rigid, treatment-resistant conditions.

The planned trial enrols people aged sixteen to thirty-five whose anorexia has already relapsed. Half receive two psilocybin sessions with structured psychological support, plus usual care. The other half receive usual care alone. Safety and tolerability come first among the outcomes. Symptom change, mood, and brain-related measures are also tracked. As a protocol, the paper reports no results. It lays out a careful test of whether psychedelic-assisted therapy can be run safely in this fragile group.
plos-pone-0352646:
Guangming Shi and four colleagues test a microbe-based method for strengthening weak loess soil. Their 2026 study uses soil from China's Ili River Valley. That loess is loose, salty, and prone to collapse and erosion. The technique coaxes bacteria to precipitate calcium carbonate, a natural cement. Three orders of applying bacteria and cementing solution were compared in the laboratory.

Applying both solutions at once worked best. Treated samples gained roughly three-fifths more compressive strength than untreated soil. Cohesion rose by over half as well. Under the microscope, the winning method built a continuous, dense cement network. It filled voids and bridged soil particles evenly. Stepwise treatments left patchy cement instead. The authors call the work preliminary, but it points to a greener way to stabilise hazard-prone loess ground.
plos-pone-0351646:
Emily Sirotich and four colleagues lay out a plan, published in 2026, for reviewing biologics and depression in skin and joint disease. Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis are long-term immune conditions. Depression often travels with them, eroding quality of life and treatment adherence. Biologic drugs, antibodies that block specific immune signals, might ease depression by calming inflammation. The existing evidence is scattered and mixed. This plan fixes the review's methods in advance.

Searches will cover five major databases and trial lists. Randomised trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies all qualify. Depression may be counted by diagnosis or by tested questionnaires. Two reviewers will screen, extract, and grade bias independently. Where data allow, pooled risk estimates will follow. As a plan, the paper reports no results. Its discipline is the point: pre-set methods make the eventual answer about biologics and mood harder to dismiss.
plos-pone-0351546:
Ahmed Abuzaid and five colleagues map where irrigation farming could work on Egypt's desert fringe. Their 2026 study covers about thirty thousand hectares west of the Nile Delta. Newly reclaimed land is a gamble without good maps. The framework blends expert weighting, fuzzy logic, and geographic software. Terrain, soil, and groundwater layers were built from maps, field surveys, and laboratory tests. Each criterion earned a weight through structured pairwise comparisons.

The weighting proved internally consistent throughout. Salt emerged as the soil's master variable, joined by sodicity and soil depth. Groundwater feasibility hinged on potential salinity and how fast water sinks in. The final maps sort the land into potential zones for planners. Egypt is pushing farming into the desert as Nile land crowds. A transparent, repeatable suitability method keeps that expansion from wasting water and money on ground that cannot repay them.
plos-pone-0351746:
Isidro Montelongo-Alfaro and six colleagues study baby oysters settling along a Mexican river estuary. Their 2026 field study follows the eastern oyster in the Soto la Marina River, on the Gulf of Mexico. Recruitment of spat, the drifting young that must attach somewhere, decides whether populations persist. Six sites stretched from near the mouth to over twenty kilometres upstream. Collectors were checked monthly for a full year. Water temperature, salinity, oxygen, acidity, and clarity were measured beside each collection.

Only salinity separated the sites significantly. It fell steadily from the salty mouth toward fresh upstream reaches. Statistical models tied spat numbers to space, season, and conditions. Gulf estuaries on the Mexican coast are understudied compared with American ones. Local oyster fisheries and restoration projects need this baseline: where the young settle, when they arrive, and which water property sorts them. Salinity's lone starring role simplifies the monitoring managers must sustain.
plos-pone-0351846:
Ming Liu and colleagues found a protein that helps stomach cancer cells survive a common chemotherapy drug. The drug is known as 5-FU. The protein is called PTPRE, and it runs high in gastric tumors. The team studied it in cancer cells and in mouse tumor grafts. They traced how it protects the cells from a form of iron-driven cell death.

The protein switches on a chain of signals inside the cell. That chain ends at a second protein, TRIB3. With the chain active, the iron-driven death route stays shut. The drug then loses one of its ways to kill, and resistance sets in. Blocking the chain could hand the drug its power back. The work names each link, which is what drug developers need first.
plos-pone-0351946:
Lei Hua, Yongshou Tao, and Liangru Shen studied three mineral-linked blood markers across the stages of a modern syndrome. The syndrome ties heart, kidney, and metabolic disease into one tangle. Data came from over fifteen thousand adults in a United States health survey. A genetic method added a second strand. It uses inherited variants to test whether a marker may help cause disease, not just follow it.

One marker stood out: alkaline phosphatase. It climbed step by step with the syndrome's stage, from early risk to advanced disease with kidney harm. Calcium and phosphorus followed their own patterns. The genetic strand singles the enzyme out still further. A cheap, common blood test may deserve a second look as this syndrome's gauge. Stage-aware markers help doctors read a condition that otherwise blurs into its parts.
plos-pone-0341246:
Disposable dishes and tubes used in fertility treatment can carry fever-causing contamination that standard checks may miss. Hiroyuki Tomari and colleagues measured such contamination, called pyrogens, across twenty products used in assisted reproduction, in this 2026 PLOS One study using a test based on human cells.

Seven products carried clear amounts of contamination, in some cases above levels once reported as safe for embryo work. A low-temperature gas treatment mixing ozone and hydrogen peroxide wiped the contamination out. Leftover peroxide on one dish type vanished after a day of drying, and treated items did not harm sperm or embryos in checks.
plos-pone-0350746:
The surface layer of joint cartilage meets joint fluid first and takes the first wear. Fengrui Liu and colleagues grew these surface cells in dishes, then stressed them with inflammatory signals and repeated stretching to mimic early osteoarthritis, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Inflammation dimmed the cells' stem-like markers and switched on several inflammatory pathways plus a cartilage-chewing enzyme. Adding stretch raised a force-sensing channel on the cells, sharpened their calcium responses, and broke down their inner skeleton. Under combined stress the cells destroyed more matrix and died more readily. The authors say protecting this front-line layer may be key to slowing joint disease early.
plos-pone-0351146:
Zaixin Wu, Xinyi Liu, and Xiaobo Han grew tiny brain like organoids from autism related cells and bathed them for a week in two gut made fatty acids, acetate and butyrate. Gut chemistry has been tied to brain development, yet direct tests are scarce. Gene activity across the whole organoid was read and grouped by function and pathway.

Acetate mainly shifted genes for gene control, catalysis, and membrane flow. Butyrate switched on immune linked processes and a key immune signalling pathway. Two similar gut chemicals thus push developing brain tissue in very different directions. Dose and timing in early life may matter for how gut health shapes the brain.
plos-pone-0348346:
Carlos Salvador-Huerta and colleagues in Spain published a trial plan in 2026 for fibromyalgia, a long-term condition of widespread pain and tiredness. Exercise helps, but pain, fear of movement, and poor body sense keep many patients from sticking with it. No results are reported yet.

Patients will follow a full virtual reality exercise program that tricks the eyes about how the body moves. The plan is to test whether that altered feedback eases pain and improves daily function better than usual care. If it works, clinics could offer a form of exercise that feels safer to people who expect movement to hurt.
plos-pone-0349646:
Leonardo F Reginato and Simon J Brandl built a computer vision tool in 2026 for tiny reef fish that hide near the bottom. These fish are hugely varied and important, yet only a handful of experts can name them from photos, so most go uncounted.

Their system, CryptoVision, learns from high quality images and answers at three levels at once: family, genus, and species, respecting how those levels nest. A design that lifts weak image features helps it separate look-alike species. If the tool proves accurate in wider use, divers and camera surveys could track these hidden fish at a scale expert time alone could never reach.
plos-pone-0349946:
Christian Raphael and colleagues ran a trial across several centres in 2026 on a soft airway tube for gut endoscopy under sedation. Patients breathe on their own while sedated, and dips in oxygen that force staff to act are common.

More than three hundred patients were split at random between care with a nasal airway tube and usual care. The main count was any airway rescue or oxygen dip. Satisfaction of patients and staff, side effects, and the role of sleep apnoea risk were also tracked. A cheap tube that cuts rescue moves would make a routine procedure safer and calmer.
plos-pone-0347346:
Xue Zhang and co-authors studied doctor photos on a large Chinese online medical platform in 2026. Patients choosing a doctor online lean on first impressions from profile pictures and reviews, and the team asked whether faces sway real bookings.

Data on more than seven thousand doctors were gathered, and software scored facial traits such as attractiveness and smiling. Attractive, smiling doctors drew higher rates of patients moving to offline visits, and doctor gender mattered too. Satisfaction reviews changed some of these links. The results raise fair minded questions for platforms, since a face is not a measure of medical skill.
plos-pone-0350646:
Daniele Capitanio and co-authors profiled proteins across metamorphosis in the sea squirt Ciona in 2026. The animal starts as a swimming larva with a simple spinal cord, then settles and dissolves most of its nervous system, a natural model of nerve loss.

Protein samples from swimming, settled, and mid change larvae were compared by mass measurement. Four hundred five proteins shifted across the stages, and network analysis grouped them by job. The catalogue shows which systems are dismantled and which built as the adult forms. Chordate cousins of vertebrates, sea squirts let researchers watch a nervous system taken apart by design.
plos-pone-0350446:
Correction notice: Shintaro Imamura and his team issued this 2026 fix to their past study of zebrafish and blood growth. Two figure panels had been copied by error when the figures were built. The team has now replaced them. The notice says the counts behind the figures do not change. It also adds ethics approvals and drug details that were left out the first time. The raw images and data for the fixed figures are posted with the notice.

The first study found that blocking a gene called telomerase left zebrafish embryos short of blood cells. The cells also failed to mature as they should. That result pointed to a side job for the gene, past guarding chromosome ends. The fix leaves those claims as they were.
plos-pone-0350046:
Fereshteh Shafiei led a lab test of ways to shield tooth enamel after radiation care. Radiation for head and neck cancers softens enamel. Acid then eats into teeth fast. The team used sixty enamel pieces cut from pulled molars. Most pieces got six weeks of radiation, in daily doses like those patients get. Four treatments were then tried on the weakened enamel.

All four treatments left enamel harder than no treatment did. A mineral paste worked best, alone or with a resin coat. It even raised hardness past the post-radiation level. A curcumin-based treatment also did well. The team says such coats may guard the teeth of cancer patients.
plos-pone-0350146:
Miena Meek Hall, Katherine R Standish, and co-authors convened focus groups of physician leaders to ask what large American health systems get right and wrong about breastfeeding care. Lactation medicine has grown as a specialty, yet families still meet patchy support because standards for organizing the care barely exist. Their 2026 study ran three focus groups with thirteen leaders working inside big health systems.

Leaders said systems should model good practice, and noted that executives' and staff members' own breastfeeding experiences sway policy more than expected. They recommended dedicated lactation divisions, better staff training, coordinated services, and support for employees who pump at work. Barriers included care split across departments, weak billing for lactation services, and low priority in training programs. Teamwork across professions and sensible record workflows were named as helpers.
plos-pone-0349246:
Michiko Hirata and colleagues measured how Venus flytrap leaves snap shut, one of the fastest moves in the plant world. A trap closes in under a second, yet how leaf size relates to leaf bending was unclear. The team filmed closing traps and scanned leaves with micro CT imaging to rebuild their shapes in three dimensions.

Faster closing came with a higher shape index. The scans also showed that bigger leaves bend by a different amount than smaller ones, a link the authors call a size and curvature constraint. They then built a two-layer model that reproduces the bending. The design rules could help engineers shape soft robots and other bending surfaces.
plos-pone-0349146:
Mateusz Gruzewski and Marek Palkowski wrote a fast computer program for predicting how an RNA molecule folds, a classic problem in computational biology. Their code implements the Nussinov algorithm, which finds the fold with the most paired bases, a task whose cost explodes as sequences grow. The trick is reorganizing the calculation so modern processors can use their memory caches and many cores well.

By splitting easy and hard cases and arranging the work like matrix multiplication, the code vectorizes cleanly and scales across very large thread counts on both major processor brands. It beat compiler-generated versions in tests. Folding speed is a bottleneck in RNA research, so a reusable, well-tuned template helps every related algorithm.
plos-pone-0337646:
Saima Sultana and colleagues built a computer model that recognises medical actions from depth sensor data, even when the room is poorly lit. Ordinary cameras struggle in dim light, and a robot that misreads a medical action could cause real harm. Their model, called I2I, works from depth readings rather than colour images, pulling out the most telling features before classifying what a person is doing.

Tested on a large public dataset of recorded actions, the model reached just over ninety-one percent accuracy and beat earlier methods the authors compared it against. The work matters for hospital and care robots that must keep working through the night or in dark wards. The authors frame depth sensing as a way to keep recognition reliable when lighting cannot be trusted.
plos-pone-0348946:
Mohammed H Alshamrani and colleagues surveyed four hundred and sixty-five parents of toddlers in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh region about tooth decay in young children and how they bottle-feed. Early childhood caries is rampant in the kingdom, and parents control the sugar, brushing, and dental visits that decide it. A structured questionnaire scored knowledge and habits across family types.

Knowledge landed in the middle range, with one glaring hole: barely one parent in eight knew when the first dental visit should happen, though most valued brushing and repairing baby teeth. Night-time bottles were the norm, and most children stayed on bottles past their first birthday. Better knowledge tracked with brushing after feeds and earlier weaning, and with mothers' education and income. The authors call for parent education that starts with that first-visit message.
plos-pone-0347046:
Elena Capelli and co-workers follow how babies learn to blend what they see and hear when someone talks. Babies at higher likelihood of autism were compared with babies at typical likelihood at six, nine, and twelve months old. Their 2026 study uses eye tracking and a classic effect where mismatched lip movements change the sound a viewer thinks they hear.

Across both groups, babies shifted their gaze from the eyes toward the mouth over the first year. Babies in the higher-likelihood group made that shift more slowly. At age two, babies showing signs linked to autism had shown the flattest shift as infants. Watching this early gaze path could help spot babies who may need extra support sooner.
plos-pone-0326546:
Amanda Tristao Santini and co-workers chart the gut bacteria of Brazilian stingless bees and where each kind lives along the gut. Stingless bees matter as pollinators, and their microbes aid food use and defense. Their 2026 study sequences gut bacteria from several species in one large genus and dissects one species region by region to map its inner tenants.

Five bacterial groups ruled the gut, arranged in a striking pattern. The crop and stomach-like parts favored some groups, while the rear gut held others plus a likely new partner species. Two famous honeybee symbionts were missing entirely. These bees run a different inner ecosystem from their better-known cousins, which hive care and conservation should respect.
plos-pone-0348446:
Abdiweli Mohamed Abdi and colleagues interviewed four hundred twenty-seven women at Banadir Hospital in Mogadishu, Somalia about what happens to leftover and expired medicines at home. Such stockpiles invite accidental poisoning, misuse, and pollution when binned. The 2026 survey found the habits widespread and risky.

Nearly everyone kept unused medicines at home, mostly for emergencies, and a third also kept expired ones. Almost nobody read storage instructions, and most never checked expiry dates before buying or swallowing a drug. More than ninety percent threw old medicines in household trash. The authors call for public education and a national take-back scheme for unwanted drugs.
plos-pone-0347146:
Abdoul Kader Ilboudo and colleagues measured exposure to Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, a dangerous tick-borne virus, in farming households of rural Burkina Faso. They tested more than seven hundred people and nearly twenty-three hundred cattle, sheep, and goats across sixteen villages, following a One Health approach that treats human and animal health as one system.

About three percent of people carried antibodies, against over half of cattle, showing the virus circulates widely in livestock. Older animals, longer grazing, and tick infestation raised exposure, and results clustered strongly within households. Sloppy livestock biosecurity raised farmers' own risk. The authors call for tick control and safer animal handling.
plos-pone-0347646:
Anastasia N. L. Newman and three co-workers set out a plan to map a gap in care. Folk who leave the ICU often bear weak limbs, fogged minds, and low mood for years. Tricks that help folk steer their own care work well in other long ills. But they are rare here, and no one has charted the work. This paper is a plan for that chart.

The team will search six stores of past work. They will keep work on grown ICU stays of a day or more that used self-steer tricks. Two staff will screen each find, with a third to break ties. The chart should show what is known and where the holes are.
plos-pone-0348146:
Radfan Saleh Abdullah, Naif Taleb Ali, and Mansour Abdelnabi H. Mehdi report a medical puzzle from war-torn Yemen: non-smokers looked far more likely to have abnormal blood haemoglobin than smokers, the reverse of normal biology. Smoking usually raises haemoglobin. They studied six hundred university students, collecting blood tests, smoking histories, and social background measures.

The reversal was real in the data and strongest among poorer students and women. Much of it ran through nutrition: in a famine-shadowed economy, being able to smoke marked relative wealth and better food. Sensitivity checks said hidden bias would have to be huge to erase the finding. The authors frame wealth as a fundamental cause that can flip biology.
plos-pone-0342546:
Zhaoying Qi and colleagues evaluate gel patches made from a partly neutralized plastic polymer in this 2026 PLOS ONE materials paper. Such gels back medicated skin patches, and their feel, stiffness, and stability depend on how the polymer chains are cross-linked. The team prepared four variants using two common acid-to-salt ratios.

Over thirty days, quality checks and flow tests showed no meaningful drift in any variant. Odor-sensing instruments, frozen microscopy, and heat-based chemical analysis found that patches with equal neutralization behaved alike, separating which recipe choices matter and which do not. For manufacturers, stable, predictable gel behavior is the difference between a patch that sticks and performs and one that fails on the shelf.
plos-pone-0347846:
SiWei Wei, Yang Yang, and ChunZhi Wang propose a new traffic forecasting network in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Road sensors form groups, not just pairs: one jam can involve a whole interchange at once. Standard graph models, which link only pairs of points, miss those group relationships, so the authors use hypergraphs that connect many nodes in a single link.

A transformer component, fitted with a time-distilling step, reads the global rhythm of flow across the network, and attention channels fuse the spatial and temporal views. Tested on two California highway datasets with repeated runs and strict statistics, the model aimed for accuracy that survives scrutiny, the standard city traffic systems need before trusting predictions.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Few Council texts on the Middle East are quoted as often as Resolution 446. It was adopted on 22 March 1979 by twelve votes to none. Norway, Britain, and the United States abstained. Jordan's ambassador had just addressed the members about Israeli settlements in occupied Arab land.

The Council ruled that building those settlements had no legal validity. It called them a serious block to a just and lasting peace. It said the Fourth Geneva Convention covers the territories taken in 1967, including Jerusalem. Israel was told to stop moving its own civilians into them. A three-member commission was created to inspect the settlement situation and report by 1 July 1979.

A new UN body took shape at the end of 2005. The Peacebuilding Commission would help states heal after wars. It was born the same week as its twin text, Resolution 1645. Resolution 1646, passed on 20 December 2005, set the Council's own stake in the new body.

The five veto powers would sit on the steering group as of right. The Council would also pick two of its rotating members each year. Those picks would join the same group. One more rule was set. The body's yearly report would come to the Council too. Members would debate it once a year. The text is short and dry. It still fixed the Council's seat at the table of the UN's newest organ.

Katanga's split from Congo pushed the young UN to a hard call. The rich province had broken away in July 1960. Belgian troops still stood on its soil. UN men had been kept out of Katanga though they stood ready to go in. The chief's new report told the tale. Resolution 146 passed on 9 August 1960 by nine votes to none. France and Italy held back.

Belgium had to pull its troops out of Katanga at once. The chief would set the pace and the way. The UN force's entry to Katanga was ruled a must. One guard rail was set down with care. The force would not take sides in Congo's own fights. It would not tip the scales of any home clash. All states were told to back the Council's word in full.

Resolution 46, adopted on 17 April 1948 by nine votes to none with two abstentions, tries to arrange a truce in Palestine. Britain still held the Mandate and was responsible for order, while fighting between Arab and Jewish forces was growing. The Council had already called for a truce two weeks earlier and now set out concrete measures.

All groups in Palestine were called on to stop military and paramilitary activity, violence, terrorism, and sabotage at once. Armed bands and fighters were not to be brought in from outside. The text pressed both leadership bodies in particular, the Arab side's Higher Committee and the Jewish Agency, to cooperate. The step was meant to guard the country's future while its political fate stayed undecided.

Resolution 1946, adopted on 15 October 2010, renews the sanctions regime on Côte d'Ivoire on the eve of a long-delayed presidential vote. An arms embargo, a ban on rough diamond exports, and targeted travel and financial measures had been in place since 2004 and 2005. Experts monitoring the regime had reported in 2009 and 2010, and a certified voters list was finally ready.

The Council kept the measures in force and extended the mandate of the experts group, judging that sanctions still supported the peace process as the first-round election approached on 31 October. It pressed Ivorian leaders to hold the vote on schedule, in open and fair conditions. Weeks later the disputed result plunged the country into crisis anyway.

Namibians seized and tried by South Africa are the cause taken up in Resolution 246, passed by a full vote on 14 March 1968. Pretoria had seized men from South West Africa and tried them under its own laws. Yet the Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966. The UN had taken charge of the land on paper. A vote in January had told South Africa to stop the trial.

South Africa did not stop. The Council voiced its distress at this defiance. It treated the arrests, the trial, and the jail terms as unlawful acts. It pressed for the men to be freed and sent home. The case became proof of the UN claim that Namibia was not South Africa's to rule.

On 17 March 1992 the Council passed Resolution 746 by a full vote. It backs a truce in Somalia that was fraying at the edges. The warring clans had signed a ceasefire pact in Mogadishu on 3 March. It let a UN team watch the truce on the ground. A UN report of 11 March warned that the clans had not kept their word. Aid could not reach the starving in safety.

The Council deplored the broken pledge and the scale of the pain the war caused. It backed the UN chief's plans for help. A small team would go first to work out a watch force. Aid flights and food convoys would grow. In a month the Council set up its first Somalia force.

Sierra Leone's fragile ceasefire frames Resolution 1346, adopted on 30 March 2001. Fighting ran along the borders with Guinea and Liberia, and refugees faced grave hardship. The UN Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, was growing under a revised plan. The Council deplored abuses by the Revolutionary United Front, including forced recruitment of adults and children, and said the Abuja Ceasefire Agreement was not being kept in full.

The Council extends UNAMSIL for six months and raises its military strength to 17,500, including 260 observers already in place. It demands that the RUF free UN movement across the country, return seized weapons and gear, and rejoin the disarmament program. It urges the government to restore civil services across its land and pushes for quick setup of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the Special Court planned under Resolution 1315.

Piracy off Somalia is fought at sea under Resolution 1846, adopted on 2 December 2008. Attacks threatened aid deliveries and shipping lanes. The Monitoring Group found escalating ransom payments were fuelling more piracy. Somalia's Transitional Federal Government asked for the Resolution 1816 (2008) powers to be renewed. The EU was about to launch a 12-month naval operation protecting World Food Programme convoys.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decides that for 12 months, states and regional organizations cooperating with the Somali government may enter Somalia's territorial waters. They must have its consent, notified in advance. They may use all necessary means there to repress piracy and armed robbery, as international law allows on the high seas. It urges naval deployments, seizure of pirate boats and equipment, shared information, and cooperation on jurisdiction and prosecution. The authorization is limited to Somalia and sets no precedent in customary law.

Resolution 1546 was adopted by the Security Council on 8 June 2004. It endorsed Iraq's return to full sovereignty after the occupation period. It welcomed the new Interim Government of Iraq, which was to take full authority on 30 June 2004. It also backed a set timetable toward elections and a permanent constitution.

The resolution gave the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, known as UNAMI, a leading role in helping Iraq. UNAMI was to help with a national conference, elections, and talks on a constitution. The resolution also kept the multinational force in Iraq, at the new government's request, with power to act for security. It set that mandate to end once the political transition was complete.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 46, adopted on 11 December 1946, pushed the rebuilding of areas wrecked by war. The Assembly backed the Economic and Social Council's plans. Among them were studies of rebuilding in Europe and in Asia and the Far East. It urged members, councils, and agencies to do all they could toward a fast fix.

The text tells the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, through the Secretary-General, that it should reach full working order at the earliest date. That way it could lend for rebuilding early in 1947. It also backs a survey of raw material needs. It backs early thought to setting up economic commissions for Europe and for Asia and the Far East.

Resolution 69/46 of the General Assembly promotes confidence-building measures between neighboring states. It reaffirms the Charter's rules against the use or threat of force and for settling disputes peacefully. It restates the methods for confidence- and security-building set out by the Disarmament Commission in 1993. Member states are called on to pursue those methods through sustained talks and dialogue. They are called on to comply strictly with their arms agreements. They are called on to build bilateral and regional measures. Those measures prevent conflict and accidental outbreaks of fighting.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1046, adopted on 13 February 1996, adjusts UNPREDEP, the United Nations Preventive Deployment Force in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Its mandate ran to 30 May 1996. The Council authorizes 50 more military personnel, so the force can keep its engineering work going. It backs the creation of a Force Commander position. It asks the Secretary-General for fresh advice on the makeup, strength and mandate by 20 May 1996.

Rough diamonds from Sierra Leone stay banned for six more months under this text of 4 December 2002. Illegal diamond trading had helped fuel the country's civil war. Though the war had ended and security had improved, large volumes of diamonds still moved outside government control.

The measures stay in force from 5 December 2002, with one standing exception. Rough diamonds certified under the government's Certificate of Origin regime remain exempt from the ban. At the end of the period the Council would review the situation, including how far government authority reached over the diamond areas, before deciding whether to extend or change the measures.

Afghanistan's assistance mission, UNAMA, is extended for a further year on 23 March 2007. The Afghanistan Compact, endorsed in 2006, set the shared plan for the country's security, governance, and development. A Council mission had visited Afghanistan in November 2006, and its report fed into this renewal.

UNAMA's mandate stays as laid out the year before, covering political support, human rights, aid coordination, and counternarcotics. Afghan parties are called on to join an inclusive political process, and the government to press ahead with reform, justice, and the fight against the drug trade. All sides are told to respect humanitarian law and protect aid workers, and donors are urged to deliver on their pledges.

The buffer force between Egypt and Israel was reviewed by the Council in the spring of 1974. The United Nations Emergency Force had been set up after the October war of 1973. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 1 April 1974, held that the force was still required. Resolution 346 was adopted on 8 April 1974.

The Council thanked the states that had sent troops to the force. It also thanked those that had given money and material. The force was praised for its contribution to the search for a just and durable peace. The Council noted a shared view about the recent disengagement of forces. Pulling Egyptian and Israeli troops apart was only a first step toward a settlement. The plan to keep the force's size under review was welcomed, so it could be cut when conditions allowed.
un-sc-res-1646:
A new Peacebuilding Commission was taking shape at the end of 2005. Resolution 1645 had created it that same day, 20 December 2005. This companion text settled the Security Council's seats on its steering body. The Council decided that all five permanent members would sit on the Organizational Committee. Two elected Council members would join them each year. The Council would pick those two annually.

The Commission's yearly report would also go to the Council. The Council would hold an annual debate on it. The body was meant to help countries recover after war. Its steering committee mixed Council, Assembly, and other members. This resolution fixed the Council's share of that mix.
un-sc-res-146:
Belgium's troops in Katanga defied the Council in the summer of 1960. The Congo's richest province had broken away with Belgian support. On 9 August 1960 the Council confirmed the Secretary-General's authority under its July resolutions. It then called on Belgium to pull its troops out of Katanga at once. The pace and manner of the withdrawal were for the Secretary-General to settle. Belgium also had to help carry out the Council's decisions in every way.

The entry of the United Nations Force into Katanga, the Council declared, was necessary. At the same time, that force could not take sides in Congo's internal fights. It could not be used to sway any conflict's outcome. That line shaped the mission's hardest years.
un-sc-res-46:
Fighting between Arabs and Jews in Palestine brought a truce call from the Security Council on 17 April 1948. Resolution 43 (1948) had opened talks with the Jewish Agency and the Arab Higher Committee. Britain, as the Mandatory Power, still bore responsibility for peace and order. The Council said an immediate halt to the violence was of the utmost urgency.

The Council called on all persons and groups in Palestine to cease military and paramilitary action, violence, terrorism, and sabotage. No armed bands or fighters were to enter Palestine, and no weapons were to be brought in or bought. Both sides had to avoid political acts that might prejudice the other community's claims while the General Assembly weighed Palestine's future government. They were told to cooperate with the Mandatory authorities on law, order, transport, health, and food and water supplies, and to keep the Holy Places safe and open.
un-sc-res-1946:
Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions were renewed on 15 October 2010, weeks before a long-delayed presidential vote. The voters list had been certified, and the first round was set for 31 October 2010 under the Ouagadougou Political Agreement. The Council noted the expert group's reports on the arms embargo. It also recorded continuing abuses against civilians, including sexual violence, despite a better overall human rights picture.

The Council renewed the arms, finance, and travel measures of resolution 1572 (2004) and the diamond ban of resolution 1643 (2005) to 30 April 2011. It promised a review tied to progress in the elections and the peace process. Ivorian parties and all states had to apply the measures in full and give inspectors free access. The Council underlined that it was ready to impose targeted measures on persons named by its committee. It also flagged media reports inciting violence and a return to civil war.
un-sc-res-246:
South Africa's trial of South West African detainees drew censure from the Security Council on 14 March 1968. Resolution 245 (1968) had ordered Pretoria to stop the illegal trial and free the men. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate over the territory in 1966 and taken direct responsibility for it. South Africa refused to comply and went on with the trial and sentencing.

The Council censured South Africa for flagrant defiance of resolution 245 and of the United Nations itself. It demanded that the South West Africans be released and sent home at once. Member states were called to help the Council give the resolution effect. The Council warned it would meet again to weigh further steps if South Africa still refused. The text treats the trial as an illegal act against people under direct United Nations responsibility.
un-sc-res-746:
Somalia's famine and fighting drew the Security Council's first steps toward intervention on 17 March 1992. Cease-fire agreements had been signed at Mogadishu on 3 March, with a United Nations monitoring mission in view. The factions had not kept the truce, and aid still could not reach people in need. The Secretary-General had reported on 11 March on the scale of the suffering.

The Council urged the Somali factions to honor the Mogadishu cease-fire at once. All factions were told to work with the Secretary-General and clear the way for aid delivery. He was asked to press his humanitarian effort with every resource he had. Member states and aid groups were appealed to for contributions. The Council backed his decision to send a technical team to Somalia at once. The team would also plan safe aid delivery. All parties had to protect aid staff.
un-sc-res-1346:
UNAMSIL was enlarged to its peak strength on 30 March 2001. Fighting still burned along the borders with Guinea and Liberia, and its human toll was grave. The Secretary-General's report of 14 March set out a revised concept of operations. The Abuja ceasefire of November 2000 was being breached, and reports of abuses by the Revolutionary United Front troubled the Council.

The Council extended UNAMSIL's mandate for six months. It raised the mission's military strength to 17,500, counting the 260 military observers already in place. The new concept of operations was welcomed. Troop-giving states won thanks for the added soldiers and support. The Secretary-General had to report at regular times on the mission's progress with the core parts of its work. Deep concern was voiced at the RUF's abuses and at its breaches of the ceasefire. The bigger force was meant to hold the peace while disarmament finally began.
un-sc-res-1846:
Piracy off Somalia occupied the Council on 2 December 2008, when it adopted Resolution 1846 on Piracy off Somalia. Growing ransom payments were fueling more attacks. Somalia's government could not patrol its own waters or guard the sea lanes. Many states and the European Union had sent warships to escort food aid convoys.

The Council renews the anti-piracy powers for twelve more months. States working with Somalia's government may enter its waters to stop piracy. They may use all necessary means there, as the law of the sea allows on the high seas. Pirate boats and gear may be seized. States should share news of attacks, help coastal states build patrol strength, and work together on trials for captured pirates.
un-sc-res-1546:
On the Council's agenda, Iraq drew Resolution 1546, adopted unanimously on 8 June 2004. The occupation authority was about to hand power to a sovereign interim government. That handover was set for 30 June 2004. Baghdad had asked the multinational force to stay on.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council endorses the interim government and the timetable that follows. Elections to a transitional assembly are due by January 2005. A permanent constitution and an elected government are to follow by the end of 2005. The force may take all necessary measures to keep security, working in partnership with Baghdad. The UN mission will lead on election advice and national dialogue.
un-sc-res-446:
Israeli settlements are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 446, adopted on 22 March 1979 by twelve votes to none, with three abstentions. Jordan had brought the matter to the Council. Building had spread across land taken in the 1967 war, including Jerusalem. The Council saw the growth of settlements as a block to peace.

The Council holds that the settlement policy and practice have no legal validity. It says the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 covers the occupied Arab lands. Israel must undo past steps and change nothing in the lands' status or makeup. Moving its own civilians into those lands must stop. A three-member panel will study the settlements and report by 1 July 1979.
europmc-pmc10066346:
Kim reviews how short-chain fatty acids made by gut microbes shape immune tolerance and autoimmunity, in a 2023 paper. These fatty acids form when gut bacteria ferment fiber from food. Immune tolerance is the system that stops the body from attacking itself, and it is built and tuned across a lifetime.

The review explains how the fatty acids calm some immune cells and guide others. It links weak production of these acids to higher risk of autoimmune disease. The paper connects diet, gut microbes, and immune balance in a clear chain.
europmc-pmc10324146:
Ye and co-authors reviewed breast cancer care in 2023, with a focus on two newer forms of treatment. Breast cancer is the second top cause of cancer death in women. Its many forms make it hard to treat with one plan. Targeted drugs aim at one molecule that helps a tumour grow.

Ye lists targets now in use, such as CDK proteins and PARP, an enzyme that fixes DNA. Some drugs have won FDA approval, alone or with other drugs. One hard form, called triple-negative, still resists targeted drugs. For that form, Ye points to immune therapy, such as drugs that lift brakes on immune cells.
europmc-pmc10434946:
Chari and Pachter argued in 2023 that a standard chart in single-cell gene studies misleads users. The chart squeezes data with hundreds or thousands of measures into a flat 2D plot. Such plots open most papers in this field and guide first looks at the data. The authors test how much truth survives that squeeze.

Their checks show the squeeze warps the data in deep ways. Cells that look close on the plot may sit far apart in the full data. Chari found that habits in making these plots vary and can flip the tale a plot seems to tell. They urge targeted plots built for one clear question instead. Broad all-in-one plots, they say, block real finds more than they help.
europmc-pmc1069646:
Foster and a large team read the full genome in 2005 of a bacterium that lives inside a parasitic worm. The worm, Brugia malayi, infects humans and causes filarial disease of skin and lymph. Its tenant, Wolbachia, is a bacterium the worm needs to breed and live. Killing the tenant may thus kill the worm.

The tenant genome is small and worn, with many genes lost. Foster found it kept key paths to make riboflavin, heme, and DNA building blocks. Those gifts may be its main pay to the host worm. The worm in turn feeds it amino acids. Next to its kin in fruit flies, this tenant lacks virus bits and repeat DNA. The map gives fresh targets to end the disease.
europmc-pmc10763046:
Iqbal and co-authors reviewed in 2024 how oxidative stress feeds cancer through cell signals and gene switches. Stress from reactive oxygen can break DNA and warp the signals that steer cell growth. High levels push cells to drop normal jobs and gain cancer traits. The team traced which paths carry that push.

Named paths include the guard gene p53, the Keap1-NRF2 stress reply, and RB1 and p21, two brakes on cell division. Iqbal shows how faults in each can free growth, blunt DNA repair, and dodge cell death. Care ideas aim to reset the redox balance, the cell's stress ledger. Antioxidant drugs and redox-tuned agents lead that work. Proof in patients is the next test.
europmc-pmc10781646:
Cui and colleagues built a reference map of how immune cells react to signal proteins in this 2024 paper. Cytokines are small proteins that cells use to send messages to each other. They guide immune responses and are targets for many drugs. No one had charted how each cell type answers each cytokine in one place.

Working in mouse lymph nodes, the team tested 86 cytokines on more than 17 cell types. Most cytokines sparked a distinct response in each cell type, they found. The data revealed over 66 driven cell states, some never described before. The team also made free software that reads gene activity data and infers which cytokines are at work. They used it to map signals in tumours after a common cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc11075546:
Sternberg and a large team report the state of the main worm genetics database in this 2024 paper. WormBase has held genome and genetics data on the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans for over two decades. The worm is a staple lab animal for studying development and disease. The team states three goals: stay current, link better with other resources, and stay sustainable.

The paper describes WormBase as it stands and the plan to move its core systems into the Alliance of Genome Resources. The Alliance is a shared infrastructure for model organism databases. As a member, WormBase will keep curating key findings from papers and large projects. It will also keep building features the worm community needs. The move is framed as a way to cut duplicated effort across databases.
europmc-pmc11299546:
Gaser and colleagues introduce a toolbox for measuring brain structure from MRI scans in this 2024 paper. Brain morphometry quantifies features such as cortical thickness and folding from magnetic resonance images. Many sophisticated tools exist, but they often demand expert handling. The Computational Anatomy Toolbox, called CAT, aims to serve beginners and experts alike through a graphical interface or scripts.

CAT covers the full workflow: preprocessing, statistical analysis, and display of results, the authors report. It supports voxel-based, surface-based, and region-based analyses, shown on an example dataset. Voxel means a 3D pixel, the smallest cube in a scan. Multiple quality control options are built in. Both one-time and repeated scans over time are handled. The paper offers the toolbox as a citable standard for the brain mapping community.
europmc-pmc11701646:
Szklarczyk and colleagues update the STRING database of protein networks in this 2025 paper. Proteins work by binding, regulating, and cooperating with each other. STRING compiles, scores, and merges evidence on protein-protein links from experiments, predictions, and prior knowledge. Its goal is a full, objective global network of physical and functional links.

Version 12.5 adds a new regulatory network. For it, the team gathers evidence on the type and direction of each regulatory link, using curated pathway databases, plus a language model fine-tuned to parse the literature. Users can now view three network types on their own: functional, physical, and regulatory. The pathway enrichment tool, which flags processes over-represented in a protein set, was also updated. Network clustering remains part of the package.
europmc-pmc11760946:
Chandimali and colleagues review free radicals and the body's antioxidant defences in this 2025 paper. Free radicals are molecules with unpaired electrons, which makes them highly reactive. They form inside the body during processes such as mitochondrial respiration, where cells burn fuel with oxygen, and immune cell activation. Outside sources include radiation, pollution, and smoking.

In balance, radicals serve cell signalling and immune defence. Overproduction breaks the balance between oxidants and antioxidants and causes oxidative stress. That stress damages DNA, proteins, and lipids. It is linked to cancer, heart disease, brain-wasting diseases, and inflammatory diseases. The review covers radical types, how they form, and their biological impacts. It also details the defence systems and ways to restore balance.
europmc-pmc1308846:
Ginaldi, Di Benedetto, and De Martinis reviewed osteoporosis through inflammation and aging in 2005. Osteoporosis thins bones and raises fracture risk in older people. Hormones, metabolism, and mechanics were the classic explanations. New evidence adds chronic inflammation as a driver.

Inflammatory signaling molecules regulate both bone-building and bone-eating cells. Aging remodels the immune system toward a more activated profile. That shift may tip bone turnover toward loss. Conditions linked to osteoporosis often share chronic inflammation too. Ginaldi reads osteoporosis partly as an inflamed aging disease. Bone loss in old age is the core concern. Old age is when the risk is at its peak for most men and women. Falls and breaks are the main harm that comes from thin bones.
europmc-pmc1363346:
Link, Shevchenko, and Heisenberg set up protein analysis for early zebrafish embryos in 2006. Zebrafish are a leading model for vertebrate development. Genetic tools were strong, but protein gel methods lagged. Yolk in embryos blocked clean protein separation.

A new method removes yolk efficiently from large embryo batches. That step enabled high-resolution 2D gel separation. Western blotting improved considerably with the same prep. Protocols run from sample prep through mass spectrometry identification. Database choices for matching zebrafish proteins were compared. Link opens protein-level study of early development. Gel steps and blot steps are spelled out in full.
europmc-pmc1821046: The Sorcerer II Global Ocean Sampling expedition: expanding the universe of protein families. — a 2005 science paper on the ocean gene trawl. It expands the protein family list. The paper is the ocean-trawl study: the findings on protein families, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1914346: Predicting nursing home admission in the U.S: a meta-analysis. — a 2005 science paper on predicting nursing-home entry. It predicts the admission odds. The paper is the admission study: the findings on nursing homes, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1940246: Effect of Body Mass Index on pregnancy outcomes in nulliparous women delivering singleton babies. — a 2005 science paper on BMI and birth outcomes. It studies the BMI effects. The paper is the BMI study: the findings on pregnancy ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1955446: Simvastatin is associated with a reduced incidence of dementia and Parkinson's disease. — a 2005 science paper on simvastatin and brain ills. It links the drug to lower odds. The paper is the simvastatin study: the findings on dementia, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2206446: Acute Kidney Injury Network: report of an initiative to improve outcomes in acute kidney injury. — a 2005 science paper on the AKIN initiative. It reports the kidney-injury initiative. The paper is the AKIN report: the findings on kidney ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2211546: Specific targeting of a plasmodesmal protein affecting cell-to-cell communication. — a 2005 science paper on plant-cell door targeting. It targets the plasmodesmal protein. The paper is the targeting study: the findings on plant ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2233646: Development of an epitope conservancy analysis tool to facilitate the design of epitope-based diagnostics and vaccines. — a 2005 science paper on an epitope-conservancy tool. It facilitates the tool design. The paper is the tool guide: the findings on epitope tools, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2289846: Genomic islands in the pathogenic filamentous fungus Aspergillus fumigatus. — a 2005 science paper on fungus gene islands. It maps the genomic islands. The paper is the island study: the findings on Aspergillus, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2374446: Rheumatic diseases in China. — a 2008 science paper on joint ills in China. It reviews the joint ills for labs worldwide. The paper is the joint-ill review: the findings on China for labs, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2375446: The adaptive evolution of the mammalian mitochondrial genome. — a 2008 science paper on cell-battery evolution. It traces the battery changes for labs. The paper is the battery study: the notes on mammal ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2440546: Phase 1 Trial of Malaria Transmission Blocking Vaccine Candidates Pfs25 and Pvs25 Formulated wi — a 2008 science paper on malaria transmission-blocking vaccines. It trials the vaccine candidates. The paper is the trial study: the findings on malaria, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2631046: Explaining adherence success in sub-Saharan Africa: an ethnographic study. — a 2008 science paper on adherence success. It explains the adherence success. The paper is the success study: the findings on Africa ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2673046: The yeast Pif1 helicase prevents genomic instability caused by G-quadruplex-forming CEB1 sequen — a 2008 science paper on the Pif1 helicase. It prevents the genomic instability. The paper is the Pif1 study: the findings on yeast ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2736946: The South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust Biomedical Research Centre (SLAM BRC) case r — a 2008 science paper on the SLAM BRC case register. It builds the case register. The paper is the register study: the findings on London ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2763246: Oxidative stress and anxiety: relationship and cellular pathways. — a 2008 science paper on oxidative stress. It studies the cellular pathways. The paper is the stress study: the findings on anxiety ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
browne-pseudodoxia-epidemica-english-164:
Thomas Browne, a Norwich doctor, published Pseudodoxia Epidemica in 1646. Its subject is vulgar errors, the false beliefs held by the common run of people. Browne examines each belief with learning, courtesy, and a doctor's questioning mind, asking how error takes root and spreads.

He tests tales about animals, plants, magnets, and pictures, and finds many wanting. His discussion of witchcraft is famous for its care and its hedges. Browne writes prose of great beauty even while doubting. The book wages learning's patient war on easy belief. It remains the classic English anatomy of error, and a model of how to question without scorn.
gaule-select-cases-of-conscience-english:
John Gaule, a minister in Huntingdonshire, published his Select Cases of Conscience in 1646. Those were the years of Matthew Hopkins, the self-styled Witchfinder General, whose hunt swept eastern England. Gaule's cases examine the scruples that witch-hunting raised in a pastor's mind, and they argue against the hunt's methods.

Gaule questions the tests, the confessions, and the haste of the finders. His protest is the first English clerical voice raised from inside the persecution itself. He wrote at real personal risk, since Hopkins's party answered critics sharply. Conscience set down in print gives the book its force. It shows resistance beginning within the church that blessed the trials.
plos-pone-0004946:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, involves long-lasting airway inflammation. Cigarette smoke is a major driver of it. Esmaeil Mortaz and co-authors studied smoke's effect on immune cells. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They exposed dendritic cells to cigarette smoke extract. Then they measured how those cells affected T cell growth.

Dendritic cells rally T cells against threats. Smoke-driven changes in them can ripple through lung immunity. The study follows that chain step by step. It links smoke exposure to altered T cell proliferation. The work shows one more way smoking distorts the lung's defenses. It also feeds the inflammation that defines COPD.
plos-pone-0005046:
Heart repair research needs large numbers of heart muscle cells. Those cells must be easy to spot and purify. Hiroko Kita-Matsuo and colleagues shared a toolkit in PLOS ONE in 2009. They built lentiviral vectors for human embryonic stem cells. Stable cell lines made with them glow for tracking. They also carry drug resistance for selection.

The protocols create lines tuned for cardiomyocyte production. Fluorescent tracking lets researchers watch heart cells develop. Drug resistance lets them select pure batches. Myocardial regeneration therapies depend on such cells. The toolkit serves development, physiology and tissue engineering studies. It removes a practical bottleneck for the whole field.
plos-pone-0005146:
The kidney filters blood and makes urine. It decides which proteins to keep and which to dump. Lulu Jia and colleagues read that decision in PLOS ONE in 2009. They compared the plasma proteome with the urine proteome. Plasma represents the kidney's input. Urine represents its output. Proteomics technology had just profiled both in detail.

Comparing the two catalogs reveals the kidney's handling rules. Some proteins pass, others are held back or reclaimed. The comparison turns two lists into insight about organ function. Many datasets had accumulated without integration. This study integrates them. The kidney's filtering logic matters for disease. Protein in urine is an early warning of kidney damage.
plos-pone-0005246:
When a soft sound comes just before a loud one, the startle response shrinks, an effect called prepulse inhibition. That gating is weak in schizophrenia and can be measured in mice. Webb and colleagues ran a genome-wide scan for it in PLOS ONE in 2009, entirely in the computer.

Large public databases hold genotypes and trait data for many inbred mouse strains. Mining them together can locate chromosome regions tied to the trait without new lab work. The in silico scan points gene hunters toward the roots of sensory gating.
plos-pone-0005346:
Trait anxiety is bred into mouse lines that run high, normal, or low in anxious behavior. Emotional information is processed differently in pathological anxiety, in people and in models. Muigg and colleagues mapped stress-induced brain activation across those lines in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Earlier rat work had already shown challenge-related activation differences in fear and anxiety circuits. The mouse maps add a second species and a three-way comparison. Consistent brain signatures of trait anxiety help researchers test calming drugs in the right circuits. Brain maps from bred lines can be checked gene by gene, since the high and low lines are known stock. And that makes them a strong test bed for new drugs for fear and stress.
plos-pone-0005946:
Cocaine changes how mammals move and behave, but the steps inside the brain are hard to trace. Alex Ward, Vyvyca Walker, Zhaoyang Feng and colleagues turned to a tiny worm for a cleaner view in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study tests how cocaine alters movement in C. elegans, a roundworm used widely in biology labs.

Cocaine blocks the pumps that clear dopamine and related signals, and the worm shares much of that machinery. If the drug shifts worm movement in clear ways, the worm can serve as a fast screen for drug action. The study brings addiction biology down to a simple animal whose genes and nerves are fully mapped.
plos-pone-0006046:
Killer cells of the immune system must learn not to attack the body's own healthy cells. Sofia Johansson, Mali Salmon-Divon, Maria Johansson and colleagues studied that schooling in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper examines natural killer cells, whose Ly49 receptors read MHC class I, the identity badges on cells, and it adds computer modeling in mice with a single badge type.

A killer cell that finds no badge may strike, a rule called missing-self recognition. During development, the host's badges educate the killers and set their restraint. Combining receptor counts with modeling shows how that education is graded, a detail that matters for using killer cells against cancer and infection.
plos-pone-0006146:
A breast cancer cell line is only as useful as the tumor it truly resembles. Jessica Kao, Keyan Salari, Melanie Bocanegra and colleagues profiled the standard lines in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses molecular profiling, including microarray data, to define which breast cancer cell lines model which forms of this varied disease, and to resource the hunt for cancer genes.

Breast cancer is many diseases in one name, and a mismatched model misleads drug tests. A profiled catalog lets labs pick the line that matches their question. The resource shapes thousands of later experiments, since almost every breast cancer drug claim begins in one of these lines.
plos-pone-0006246:
Wind turbines kill large numbers of bats, and no accepted fix existed when Barry Nicholls and Paul Racey ran their 2009 PLOS ONE study. Earlier, the team had seen bat activity drop near large air traffic and weather radars. That hint suggested radar-like signals might keep bats away.

Bats avoided foraging where electromagnetic radiation was present, the tests showed. A signal bats dislike could guard turbines without harming birds or power output. The idea needs field trials at real turbines before use. Still, it offers a rare, testable lead for a stubborn conservation problem.
